resp = legacy.generate("Explain RAG", 256)["text"]   # vendor-specific shape, scattered all over

With the pattern — callers use one clean interface; the adapter does the translation in one place:

resp = client.complete("Explain RAG")   # modern API; swap the vendor behind it freely

From-scratch:

class LegacyCompletionAPI:
    """Old vendor SDK: prompt + token budget in, dict out."""
    def generate(self, prompt_text: str, max_len: int) -> dict:
        return {"text": f"[legacy] {prompt_text[:max_len]}", "tokens": max_len}

class LegacyLLMAdapter:
    """Adapts the legacy API to our modern .complete(prompt) interface."""
    def __init__(self, legacy: LegacyCompletionAPI):
        self._legacy = legacy
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        return self._legacy.generate(prompt, max_len=256)["text"]

def ask(client, prompt):
    return client.complete(prompt)

print(ask(LegacyLLMAdapter(LegacyCompletionAPI()), "Explain RAG"))
# [legacy] Explain RAG

Vendor-adapter form — two SDKs, one interface:

from typing import Protocol

class LLMClient(Protocol):
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class OpenAIAdapter:
    def __init__(self, sdk): self._c = sdk
    def complete(self, prompt):
        r = self._c.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        return r.choices[0].message.content        # translate to our shape

class AnthropicAdapter:
    def __init__(self, sdk): self._c = sdk
    def complete(self, prompt):
        r = self._c.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-4", max_tokens=1024,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        return r.content[0].text                    # different shape → same output

When to use: Integrating third-party or legacy code with a mismatched interface, or unifying several APIs behind one expected shape.

Verdict: ✅ One of the most useful patterns in real Python. Whenever you depend on a third-party SDK, adapt it to your interface so you can swap vendors. Often just a thin class — or even a function. Pairs naturally with the Factory registry.

•

7. Bridge

IntuitioninjectsReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternFrom-scratch

Intuition: You have two things that vary independently — what the LLM task is (summarize, translate) and which backend runs it (OpenAI, local). If you make one subclass per combination you get SummarizeWithOpenAI, SummarizeWithLocal, TranslateWithOpenAI, … — an explosion. Bridge keeps them as two separate dimensions and injects the "how" (backend) into the "what" (task), so you have N + M classes instead of N × M.

Real-world: An LLM task abstraction (Summarize, Translate, Classify) that delegates generation to a separate LLMBackend (OpenAIBackend, AnthropicBackend, LocalBackend). Add tasks and backends independently — no SummarizeViaOpenAI, TranslateViaLocal… explosion.

Without the pattern — one subclass per (task × backend) pairing:

class SummarizeWithOpenAI: ...
class SummarizeWithLocal: ...
class TranslateWithOpenAI: ...
class TranslateWithLocal: ...   # N tasks × M backends classes to maintain

With the pattern — inject the backend; tasks and backends vary independently:

Summarize(OpenAIBackend())
Summarize(LocalBackend())     # N + M classes, not N × M

From-scratch:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class LLMBackend(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def generate(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class OpenAIBackend(LLMBackend):
    def generate(self, prompt): return f"[gpt-4o] {prompt}"
class LocalBackend(LLMBackend):
    def generate(self, prompt): return f"[llama-local] {prompt}"

class LLMTask(ABC):
    def __init__(self, backend: LLMBackend): self.backend = backend
    @abstractmethod
    def run(self, text: str) -> str: ...

class Summarize(LLMTask):
    def run(self, text): return self.backend.generate(f"Summarize: {text}")
class Translate(LLMTask):
    def __init__(self, backend, lang): super().__init__(backend); self.lang = lang
    def run(self, text): return self.backend.generate(f"Translate to {self.lang}: {text}")

for backend in (OpenAIBackend(), LocalBackend()):
    print(Summarize(backend).run("a long article"))
# [gpt-4o] Summarize: a long article
# [llama-local] Summarize: a long article
print(Translate(OpenAIBackend(), "French").run("hello"))
# [gpt-4o] Translate to French: hello

When to use: Two dimensions vary independently (shape × renderer, message × transport). Bridge avoids the combinatorial explosion of one subclass per pairing.

Verdict: ⚠️ In Python this is usually just composition + dependency injection. The formal "two parallel hierarchies" structure is rarely needed. If you're injecting a Sender into a Notification, you already have the benefit without naming it Bridge.

•

8. Composite

IntuitionReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: A folder can hold files and other folders, yet you treat "give me your size" the same whether you're asking a single file or the whole tree — the folder just sums its children. Composite lets leaves and containers share one interface so callers never branch on "is this a single thing or a group?"

Real-world: A RAG corpus where a Chunk and a Document both answer .tokens() so you can total a whole collection; or a nested agent team where a single Tool and a ToolGroup both expose .run().

Without the pattern — you branch on "chunk or container?" everywhere you recurse:

def total(node):
    if isinstance(node, Document): return sum(total(c) for c in node.children)
    return node.tokens               # type checks scattered through the code

With the pattern — leaves and containers share one interface; just call the method:

corpus.tokens()   # Document sums its children, Chunk returns its own count — caller doesn't care

From-scratch — a corpus → document → chunk tree, summing token counts:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Node(ABC):
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    @abstractmethod
    def tokens(self) -> int: ...
    @abstractmethod
    def show(self, indent=0): ...

class Chunk(Node):
    def __init__(self, name, tokens): super().__init__(name); self._tokens = tokens
    def tokens(self): return self._tokens
    def show(self, indent=0): print(f"{'  '*indent}- {self.name} ({self._tokens} tok)")

class Document(Node):
    def __init__(self, name): super().__init__(name); self.children: list[Node] = []
    def add(self, node): self.children.append(node); return self
    def tokens(self): return sum(c.tokens() for c in self.children)   # recursive
    def show(self, indent=0):
        print(f"{'  '*indent}+ {self.name} ({self.tokens()} tok)")
        for c in self.children: c.show(indent + 1)

corpus = Document("corpus")
corpus.add(Document("guide.md").add(Chunk("intro", 120)).add(Chunk("setup", 80)))
corpus.add(Chunk("faq.txt", 50))
corpus.show()
# + corpus (250 tok)
#   + guide.md (200 tok)
#     - intro (120 tok)
#     - setup (80 tok)
#   - faq.txt (50 tok)
print(corpus.tokens())   # 250

When to use: Part-whole hierarchies where leaves and containers should be handled the same way — file systems, UI widget trees, org charts, scene graphs.

Verdict: ✅ Genuinely useful for real tree structures. Whenever "a thing can contain things of its own type, and you want to operate on the whole tree uniformly," this is the right model. Clean in Python via a shared Protocol/ABC + recursion.

•

9. Decorator

IntuitionwrapTwo different "decorators"objectfunctionReal-world

Intuition: You want to add a responsibility (logging, caching, retry) to an object without rewriting it or subclassing for every combination — so you wrap it in another object with the same interface that does its bit and then forwards the rest. Like gift-wrapping: the present is unchanged; the wrapper adds something on top, and you can wrap a wrapped box again.

⚠️ Two different "decorators": this is the GoF structural decorator (wrap an object). Python also has the native @decorator syntax (wrap a function). For function/method behavior, use the @ form; for object wrapping, use the class form below.

Real-world: Adding caching, retry, logging, or timing around a function (Python's @ does this natively). Generic: wrapping a data stream with compression then encryption layers.

Without the pattern — you subclass for every combination of concerns (a class explosion):

class LoggingLLM(LLM): ...        # and CachingLLM, and LoggingCachingLLM, and …

With the pattern — wrap any object at runtime and stack concerns freely:

m = LoggingLLM(CachingLLM(LLM()))   # compose layers, no subclass explosion

From-scratch — wrapping an LLM client via __getattr__ delegation:

class BaseLLM:
    def complete(self, prompt): return f"answer to: {prompt}"
    def model(self): return "gpt-4o"

class LoggingLLM:
    """Wraps any LLM client, adding logging while delegating the rest."""
    def __init__(self, inner): self._inner = inner
    def complete(self, prompt):
        print(f"-> prompt {prompt!r} on {self._inner.model()}")
        out = self._inner.complete(prompt)
        print(f"<- {out!r}")
        return out
    def __getattr__(self, attr):
        return getattr(self._inner, attr)   # delegate model(), etc.

m = LoggingLLM(BaseLLM())
m.complete("hi")
# -> prompt 'hi' on gpt-4o
# <- 'answer to: hi'
print(m.model())   # gpt-4o  (delegated)

Wrappers stack, each adding one concern (here: caching over retry):

class CachingLLM:
    def __init__(self, inner): self._inner, self._cache = inner, {}
    def complete(self, prompt):
        if prompt in self._cache:
            print("  [cache hit]"); return self._cache[prompt]
        out = self._inner.complete(prompt); self._cache[prompt] = out
        return out

class RetryLLM:
    def __init__(self, inner, times=3): self._inner, self._times = inner, times
    def complete(self, prompt):
        for _ in range(self._times):
            try: return self._inner.complete(prompt)
            except Exception: continue
        raise RuntimeError("LLM call failed after retries")

llm = CachingLLM(RetryLLM(BaseLLM()))    # retry the call, then cache the result
print(llm.complete("define RAG"))        # answer to: define RAG
print(llm.complete("define RAG"))        #   [cache hit] -> answer to: define RAG

Python function decorator (the idiomatic form for behavior):

import functools

def retry(times: int = 3):
    """Retry a function on failure — a decorator factory."""
    def decorator(func):
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            last = None
            for _ in range(times):
                try: return func(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception as exc: last = exc
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retry(times=3)
def call_llm(prompt): ...   # flaky network call, now auto-retried

When to use: Add cross-cutting concerns (logging, caching, encryption, timing) at runtime without subclass explosion.

Verdict: ✅✅ for function/method behavior use Python's native @; ✅ for object wrapping use __getattr__ delegation. Don't build wrapper-class towers when a @ decorator layers the behavior on a function directly.

•

10. Facade

Intuitionone simple front doorReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: A complicated subsystem has many moving parts; a facade is the one simple front door that hides them. Like a restaurant: you say "I'll have the set menu" and the kitchen runs ten steps you never see. The facade only orchestrates — it holds no business logic of its own.

Real-world: A RAGService.answer(query) that hides retrieve → rerank → build-prompt → generate → cite; or an IngestionFacade.ingest(path) that hides load → chunk → embed → upsert. Callers never touch the internal components.

Without the pattern — the caller orchestrates every ingestion step by hand, every time:

out = VectorDB().upsert(Embedder().embed(Chunker().chunk(Loader().load("guide.md"))))

With the pattern — one call hides the whole pipeline:

out = IngestionFacade().ingest("guide.md")

From-scratch — a document-ingestion facade (load → chunk → embed → upsert):

class Loader:   def load(self, path): return f"text of {path}"
class Chunker:  def chunk(self, text): return [text[:6], text[6:]]
class Embedder: def embed(self, chunks): return [[0.1] for _ in chunks]
class VectorDB: def upsert(self, vecs): return f"upserted {len(vecs)} vectors"

class IngestionFacade:
    """One simple call hides the multi-step ingestion pipeline."""
    def __init__(self):
        self._loader = Loader()
        self._chunker = Chunker()
        self._embedder = Embedder()
        self._db = VectorDB()
    def ingest(self, path: str) -> str:
        text = self._loader.load(path)
        chunks = self._chunker.chunk(text)
        vecs = self._embedder.embed(chunks)
        return self._db.upsert(vecs)

print(IngestionFacade().ingest("guide.md"))
# upserted 2 vectors

RAG service facade — same shape, GenAI flavor:

class RAGService:
    """Hide the multi-step RAG pipeline behind one method."""
    def __init__(self, retriever, reranker, generator):
        self._retriever, self._reranker, self._generator = retriever, reranker, generator
    def answer(self, query: str) -> str:
        docs = self._retriever.search(query, top_k=20)
        top = self._reranker.rerank(query, docs, top_k=5)
        prompt = f"Context:\n{chr(10).join(top)}\n\nQuestion: {query}"
        return self._generator.complete(prompt)

When to use: You want a clean entry point that shields callers from a sprawling subsystem (multi-step pipelines, SDK wrappers, "do the whole thing" helpers).

Verdict: ✅ Very useful and very common. Most well-designed "service" classes are Facades. The skill is keeping the facade thin — orchestration only, with no business logic leaking in.

•

11. Flyweight

IntuitiononceReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: If thousands of objects share the same heavy, unchanging data, store that data once and let them all point at the shared copy — keep only the tiny per-object difference separate. Like a print shop reusing one metal letter-stamp for every 'a' on the page rather than carving a new 'a' each time.

Real-world: Reusing one shared system prompt / tokenizer / embedding-table object across thousands of request objects instead of copying it into each — only the per-request user message differs.

Without the pattern — every request carries its own copy of the long system prompt:

reqs = [ChatRequest(msg, system="You are a helpful, terse assistant...") for msg in msgs]  # N copies

With the pattern — requests share one cached, interned instance of the common part:

system = SystemPrompt("default", LONG_SYSTEM_TEXT)   # created once, reused by all
reqs = [ChatRequest(msg, system) for msg in msgs]

From-scratch — a __new__ cache (interning) for shared system prompts:

class SystemPrompt:
    """Shared intrinsic state (the long system prompt) — interned via a cache."""
    _cache: dict = {}
    def __new__(cls, role, text):
        key = (role, text)
        if key not in cls._cache:
            inst = super().__new__(cls)
            inst.role, inst.text = role, text
            cls._cache[key] = inst
        return cls._cache[key]
    def __repr__(self): return f"SystemPrompt({self.role})"

class ChatRequest:
    def __init__(self, user_msg, system): self.user_msg, self.system = user_msg, system  # extrinsic + shared

LONG = "You are a helpful, terse assistant. Cite sources. Never invent facts."
p1 = SystemPrompt("default", LONG)
p2 = SystemPrompt("default", LONG)    # same cached object
p3 = SystemPrompt("coder", "You write Python only.")
print(p1 is p2)                        # True — shared flyweight
reqs = [ChatRequest(m, p1) for m in ["hi", "bye", "thanks"]]
print(f"Unique system-prompt objects: {len(SystemPrompt._cache)}")   # 2 (for many requests)

Pythonic version — @lru_cache on a factory + frozen dataclass:

from functools import lru_cache
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)   # immutable → safe to share
class PromptTemplate:
    name: str
    text: str

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def get_template(name: str, text: str) -> PromptTemplate:
    return PromptTemplate(name, text)

assert get_template("qa", LONG) is get_template("qa", LONG)   # same object, shared

When to use: Huge numbers of objects sharing repeating data. The shared part must be immutable — mutating a flyweight would corrupt every object referencing it.

Verdict: ⚠️ Rare — only when memory is a measured constraint. Python already interns small ints and some strings. When you do need it, @lru_cache on a factory + __slots__ on the class is the Pythonic form. Don't reach for it speculatively.

•

12. Proxy

Intuitioncontrols accessReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: A stand-in object that looks exactly like the real thing but controls access to it — to delay loading it, cache its answers, check permissions, or log calls. Like a celebrity's assistant: you talk to the assistant with the same requests, and they decide whether/when to bother the celebrity.

Real-world: Lazy-loading a heavy embedding model only on first use; wrapping an LLM client with rate-limiting, caching, or a per-tenant auth check before forwarding the call.

Without the pattern — every caller wraps the real client with its own cache bookkeeping:

if prompt in cache: out = cache[prompt]
else: out = llm.complete(prompt); cache[prompt] = out   # repeated at every call site

With the pattern — the proxy looks exactly like the real client but controls access transparently:

out = caching_llm.complete(prompt)   # caching/lazy-loading handled inside, same interface

From-scratch — a caching LLM proxy (skip the API call + token cost on repeats):

import time

class LLM:
    def complete(self, prompt: str):
        time.sleep(0.05)   # simulate a slow, paid API call
        return f"answer: {prompt}"

class CachingLLMProxy:
    def __init__(self, llm: LLM, ttl=60):
        self._llm, self._ttl, self._cache = llm, ttl, {}
    def complete(self, prompt: str):
        hit = self._cache.get(prompt)
        if hit and time.time() - hit["t"] < self._ttl:
            print(f"  cache HIT: {prompt!r}");  return hit["data"]
        print(f"  cache MISS: {prompt!r}")
        data = self._llm.complete(prompt)
        self._cache[prompt] = {"data": data, "t": time.time()}
        return data

llm = CachingLLMProxy(LLM())
llm.complete("What is RAG?")   # cache MISS
llm.complete("What is RAG?")   # cache HIT

Virtual proxy — defer expensive construction until first use:

class LazyModelProxy:
    """Defer loading the real (expensive) model until first use."""
    def __init__(self, path): self._path, self._model = path, None
    def _ensure(self):
        if self._model is None:
            print("Loading model... (happens once)")
            self._model = load_expensive_model(self._path)
    def predict(self, x):
        self._ensure()
        return self._model.predict(x)

When to use: Cross-cutting access control where the proxy must look exactly like the real object: caching, lazy/virtual loading, remote stubs, permission checks.

Verdict: ✅ Useful — heavily overlaps Decorator. Rule of thumb: Proxy controls access (lazy load, auth, caching), Decorator adds behavior. In Python, __getattr__ and @property make lazy proxies trivial; lazy-loading a heavy model on first use is the most common real case.

Structural scorecard

PatternVerdictPython note
Adapter✅thin class/function; vendor independence
Bridge⚠️usually just composition + DI
Composite✅Protocol/ABC + recursion for real trees
Decorator✅✅native @ for functions; __getattr__ for objects
Facade✅most "service" classes are this
Flyweight⚠️only on measured memory pressure
Proxy✅__getattr__ / @property; controls access

Takeaway: Structural patterns survive better than Creational ones — Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Composite, and Proxy are everyday tools. Bridge and Flyweight are situational.

Part III — Behavioral Patterns (11)

Concerned with how objects communicate and divide responsibility.

•

13. Chain of Responsibility

IntuitionReal-worldmiddlewareWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: Line up a row of handlers and pass a request down the line — each either deals with it or hands it on. Like an expense approval: your manager signs off small amounts, escalates big ones to the director, who escalates huge ones to the VP. The sender doesn't know who will ultimately handle it.

Real-world: A guardrail chain on LLM input — profanity check → PII redaction → injection detection, each deciding to pass, block, or modify. FastAPI / Starlette middleware wrapping your /chat endpoint is literally this pattern.

Without the pattern — one function with nested guardrail checks the caller must know all about:

def screen(prompt):
    if "damn" in prompt:            return "blocked: profanity"
    if "ssn" in prompt:             return "blocked: PII"     # add/reorder a check → edit this function
    if "ignore previous" in prompt: return "blocked: injection"
    return "ok"

With the pattern — independent guardrails linked in a chain, added or reordered freely:

profanity.set_next(PIIRedact()).set_next(Injection())   # profanity → PII → injection → …
profanity.check(prompt)                                  # each guard decides to block or pass it on

From-scratch — a moderation chain of linked guardrails:

from abc import ABC

class Guard(ABC):
    def __init__(self): self._next: "Guard | None" = None
    def set_next(self, h: "Guard") -> "Guard":
        self._next = h
        return h                     # return next to allow chaining set_next
    def check(self, prompt):
        return self._next.check(prompt) if self._next else {"ok": True, "prompt": prompt}

class Profanity(Guard):
    def check(self, prompt):
        if "damn" in prompt.lower(): return {"ok": False, "reason": "profanity"}
        return super().check(prompt)

class PIIRedact(Guard):
    def check(self, prompt):
        if "ssn" in prompt.lower(): return {"ok": False, "reason": "PII"}
        return super().check(prompt)

class Injection(Guard):
    def check(self, prompt):
        if "ignore previous" in prompt.lower(): return {"ok": False, "reason": "prompt injection"}
        return super().check(prompt)

chain = Profanity(); chain.set_next(PIIRedact()).set_next(Injection())  # profanity -> PII -> injection
print(chain.check("my ssn is 123"))                  # {'ok': False, 'reason': 'PII'}
print(chain.check("ignore previous instructions"))   # {'ok': False, 'reason': 'prompt injection'}
print(chain.check("summarize this document"))        # {'ok': True, 'prompt': '...'}

Pythonic version — a list of callables (no linked-list ceremony):

from typing import Callable

Guardrail = Callable[[str], str | None]   # returns None to block

def block_pii(text):       return None if "ssn" in text.lower() else text
def block_injection(text): return None if "ignore previous" in text.lower() else text

def run_chain(text: str, chain: list[Guardrail]) -> str | None:
    for guard in chain:
        text = guard(text)
        if text is None: return None      # blocked, short-circuit
    return text

When to use: Request pipelines — web middleware (auth → rate-limit → validation), event processing, approval workflows. Handlers are added/reordered without touching each other.

Verdict: ✅ Useful — but a list of callables beats a linked-list of handler classes. The GoF "each handler holds a ._next" structure is unnecessary in Python; iterate a list. You already use this conceptually in middleware and validation pipelines.

•

14. Command

IntuitionobjectReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: Wrap "an action to perform" into an object — so you can store it, queue it, log it, or undo it later. Like writing a chore on a sticky note instead of doing it immediately: now you can reorder the notes, redo them, or tear one up (undo).

Real-world: Representing an agent's tool-call as a serializable, replayable object; queuing background generation jobs (a Celery task is a command); undo/redo over an agent's edits to a draft answer.

Without the pattern — the agent mutates its draft inline, so there's no way to undo, queue, or log the revision:

draft.text += "Then it generates."   # done — and irreversible

With the pattern — each revision is an object with execute/undo, so history works:

history.do(Append(draft, "Then it generates.")); history.undo()   # reversible, queueable, loggable

From-scratch — an agent revising a draft answer, with undo:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Command(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def execute(self): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def undo(self): ...

class Draft:
    def __init__(self): self.text = ""
    def __str__(self): return self.text

class Append(Command):
    def __init__(self, draft, text): self.draft, self.text = draft, text
    def execute(self): self.draft.text += self.text
    def undo(self):    self.draft.text = self.draft.text[: -len(self.text)]

class History:
    def __init__(self): self._stack: list[Command] = []
    def do(self, cmd): cmd.execute(); self._stack.append(cmd)
    def undo(self):
        if self._stack: self._stack.pop().undo()

draft, h = Draft(), History()
h.do(Append(draft, "RAG retrieves docs. ")); print(draft)   # RAG retrieves docs.
h.do(Append(draft, "Then it generates."));  print(draft)    # RAG retrieves docs. Then it generates.
h.undo(); print(draft)                                      # RAG retrieves docs.

When to use: Undo/redo, action queues, macro recording, transactional operations.

Verdict: ⚠️ Full Command class only when you need undo / serialization / queuing. If you just need "run this later," a closure or functools.partial is the Pythonic Command. Reach for the class when commands must be inspected, stored, or reversed.

•

15. Interpreter

Intuitionevaluate itselfReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternparser

Intuition: Given a tiny language (a boolean rule, a filter expression), model its grammar as a tree of small objects, each of which knows how to evaluate itself. The rule becomes data you can build and edit — even author from text — instead of code only a programmer can change.

Real-world: A model-routing DSL ("(is_complex or is_premium) and not is_rate_limited"), a metadata-filter DSL over retrieved chunks ("source == docs and score > 0.8"), or feature-flag expressions for which tool an agent may call.

Without the pattern — the routing rule is hard-coded in Python, so only a programmer can change which model gets used:

def use_premium_model(ctx):
    return (ctx["is_complex"] or ctx["is_premium_user"]) and not ctx["is_rate_limited"]   # baked into code

With the pattern — the rule is built from composable expression objects (and can be parsed from text):

rule = And(Or(Var("is_complex"), Var("is_premium_user")), Not(Var("is_rate_limited")))
rule.interpret(ctx)   # the routing rule is data — authorable without code changes

From-scratch — a model-routing rule evaluator:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Expr(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def interpret(self, context: dict) -> bool: ...

# ── Terminal expressions ──
class Var(Expr):
    def __init__(self, key): self.key = key
    def interpret(self, ctx): return bool(ctx.get(self.key))
class Const(Expr):
    def __init__(self, value): self.value = value
    def interpret(self, ctx): return self.value

# ── Non-terminal expressions (compose other expressions) ──
class And(Expr):
    def __init__(self, l, r): self.l, self.r = l, r
    def interpret(self, ctx): return self.l.interpret(ctx) and self.r.interpret(ctx)
class Or(Expr):
    def __init__(self, l, r): self.l, self.r = l, r
    def interpret(self, ctx): return self.l.interpret(ctx) or self.r.interpret(ctx)
class Not(Expr):
    def __init__(self, op): self.op = op
    def interpret(self, ctx): return not self.op.interpret(ctx)

# Route to the premium model when: (is_complex OR is_premium_user) AND NOT is_rate_limited
rule = And(Or(Var("is_complex"), Var("is_premium_user")), Not(Var("is_rate_limited")))
print(rule.interpret({"is_complex": True,  "is_rate_limited": False}))   # True  -> use GPT-4
print(rule.interpret({"is_premium_user": True, "is_rate_limited": True})) # False -> fall back to mini

In practice a parser builds the tree from a string, so product/ops can author routing rules the interpreter evaluates at runtime.

When to use: A small, stable domain language evaluated repeatedly — boolean rule / feature-flag engines, search-query filters, formula evaluators. Each grammar rule is one class.

Verdict: ❌ Almost never roll your own grammar. Use ast, or a parsing library (lark, pyparsing). A hand-written interpreter class hierarchy is a maintenance trap for anything resembling a real language. Recognize it; rarely build it. (Contrast with Specification §M2: both model composable boolean rules, but Specification combines predicates via & | ~, while Interpreter exposes an explicit grammar/AST you can parse from text.)

•

16. Iterator

IntuitiongeneratorReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: Walk through a collection one item at a time without exposing how it's stored. Python bakes this into the language: any object with __iter__ works in a for loop, and a generator (yield) is an iterator with almost no boilerplate.

Real-world: Batching texts for the embedding API, streaming tokens from an LLM, scrolling pages of hits from a vector DB, lazily reading a huge corpus you can't fit in memory.

Without the pattern — you expose the internal storage and make every caller index it by hand:

i = 0
while i < len(b.texts):          # caller must know the layout and batch size
    print(b.texts[i:i + 2]); i += 2

With the pattern — implement __iter__; callers just loop, internals stay hidden:

for batch in EmbeddingBatches(texts, size=2):
    embed(batch)                 # send to the embedding API in batches

From-scratch — batching texts for the embedding API (generator-based, idiomatic):

class EmbeddingBatches:
    def __init__(self, texts, size=2): self.texts, self.size = texts, size
    def __iter__(self):
        for i in range(0, len(self.texts), self.size):
            yield self.texts[i:i + self.size]

for batch in EmbeddingBatches(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"], size=2):
    print("embed batch:", batch)
# embed batch: ['a', 'b']
# embed batch: ['c', 'd']
# embed batch: ['e']

Lazy pagination — never load everything at once:

from typing import Iterator

def paginate(client, page_size=100) -> Iterator[dict]:
    cursor = None
    while True:
        page = client.fetch(cursor=cursor, limit=page_size)
        yield from page["items"]
        cursor = page.get("next_cursor")
        if cursor is None: return

When to use: Custom traversal order, lazy/streaming sequences, batching, pagination.

Verdict: ❌ Dead as an explicit pattern — use generators. Python's __iter__/__next__ protocol and yield are the Iterator pattern, built in. Writing an Iterator class with has_next()/next() is a Java accent. Just yield.

•

17. Mediator

IntuitionhubReal-worldsupervisor / orchestratorWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: Instead of every object wiring up to every other object (an N×N tangle), they all talk to one hub that owns the interaction logic. Like an air-traffic controller: planes don't negotiate with each other directly; they all coordinate through the tower.

Real-world: A multi-agent supervisor / orchestrator — agents don't call each other; they report to the supervisor, which routes work (the LangGraph Supervisor pattern). The same shape powers an agent message bus where researcher/writer/critic coordinate through one hub.

Without the pattern — every agent holds a reference to every other (an N×N web of coupling):

researcher.send_to(writer, result)
researcher.send_to(critic, result)   # each agent must be wired to all the others

With the pattern — agents talk only to the hub (hub-and-spoke):

researcher.publish("found 3 sources")   # the AgentHub routes it to the rest

From-scratch — an agent hub that coordinates a researcher / writer / critic:

class AgentHub:
    """Mediator that routes messages between agents — they never call each other."""
    def __init__(self): self.agents, self.log = {}, []
    def register(self, agent):
        self.agents[agent.name] = agent; agent.hub = self
    def publish(self, sender, message, to=None):
        self.log.append(f"{sender.name}: {message}")
        if to:                                          # direct message
            if to in self.agents:
                self.agents[to].receive(message, sender.name)
        else:                                           # broadcast
            for name, agent in self.agents.items():
                if agent is not sender:
                    agent.receive(message, sender.name)

class Agent:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name, self.hub, self.inbox = name, None, []
    def publish(self, message, to=None):
        if self.hub: self.hub.publish(self, message, to)
    def receive(self, message, sender):
        self.inbox.append(message)
        print(f"  [{self.name}] from {sender}: {message}")

hub = AgentHub()
researcher, writer, critic = Agent("researcher"), Agent("writer"), Agent("critic")
for a in (researcher, writer, critic): hub.register(a)
researcher.publish("found 3 sources")       # broadcast to writer and critic
writer.publish("draft ready", to="critic")  # direct message

Supervisor (GenAI) form — agents route through a hub, not each other:

class Supervisor:
    def __init__(self): self._agents = {}
    def register(self, agent): self._agents[agent.name] = agent
    def route(self, task: str) -> str:
        if "sql" in task.lower():
            return self._agents["db_agent"].handle(task)
        return self._agents["general_agent"].handle(task)

When to use: Many objects communicate in complex ways (chat rooms, air-traffic control, multi-agent systems). Contrast with Observer: Observer is one-to-many broadcast; Mediator manages two-way, many-to-many coordination.

Verdict: ✅ Relevant — especially in multi-agent systems. A Supervisor architecture is a Mediator; it prevents the N² coupling of every agent knowing every other. The risk: the mediator becoming a god-object — keep its job to routing, not doing the work.

•

18. Memento

IntuitionsnapshotReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: Take a snapshot of an object's full state now, so you can restore it later — without exposing the object's internals. Like a video-game save file: you don't care what's inside it; you just "save" and "load."

Real-world: Checkpointing agent/graph state to resume or roll back (LangGraph checkpointing is conceptually this); snapshotting a conversation before a risky tool call so you can revert if it fails.

Without the pattern — you stash and restore each field by hand, and it breaks whenever the state grows:

saved_messages, saved_step = sess.messages[:], sess.step
sess.messages, sess.step = saved_messages, saved_step   # miss a field → corrupt restore

With the pattern — snapshot the whole state opaquely and restore it in one call:

m = sess.save(); ...; sess.restore(m)   # full agent state captured, encapsulation intact

From-scratch — checkpoint and roll back an agent session:

import copy

class Memento:
    def __init__(self, state): self._state = copy.deepcopy(state)
    @property
    def state(self): return copy.deepcopy(self._state)

class AgentSession:
    def __init__(self): self.messages, self.step = [], 0
    def send(self, msg): self.messages.append(msg); self.step += 1
    def save(self) -> Memento:
        return Memento({"messages": self.messages, "step": self.step})
    def restore(self, m: Memento):
        s = m.state; self.messages, self.step = s["messages"], s["step"]
    def __str__(self): return f"step={self.step} msgs={self.messages}"

sess, history = AgentSession(), []
history.append(sess.save()); sess.send("user: hi"); print(sess)         # step=1 msgs=['user: hi']
history.append(sess.save()); sess.send("assistant: hello"); print(sess) # step=2 msgs=[...]
sess.restore(history.pop()); print(f"Rolled back: {sess}")              # Rolled back: step=1 msgs=['user: hi']

When to use: Undo/redo where reversing each action is hard but snapshotting state is easy — editors, game saves, transactional checkpoints. Memento (snapshots) vs Command (reversible actions): use Command when the inverse is cheap, Memento when full-state capture is simpler.

Verdict: ⚠️ In Python, usually just serialize state. A dataclass / Pydantic .model_dump() round-trip is the Memento, and it's persistable to disk/Redis for free. Don't build a separate Memento + Caretaker class trio; dump and reload.

•

19. Observer

Intuitionsubscriberslist of callbacksReal-worldWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: When one object changes, a list of interested subscribers should automatically hear about it — without the subject knowing who they are. Like a newsletter: you publish one post and every subscriber gets it; you don't email each person individually. The Pythonic form is just a list of callbacks.

Real-world: Streaming token callbacks during LLM generation; per-step agent tracing/telemetry callbacks; fan-out of a "generation complete" event to logging, analytics, and a websocket push.

Without the pattern — the subject hard-codes every reaction, so adding one means editing it:

def run(self, tokens):
    for t in tokens:
        print(t); log_buffer.append(t); count_tokens(t)   # tightly coupled

With the pattern — subscribers register themselves; the subject just emits an event:

gen.on("token", to_console); gen.on("token", to_log)
gen.run(tokens)   # subject doesn't know or care who is listening

From-scratch — a streaming generation emitter (token-by-token, like an LLM stream):

from typing import Callable

class EventEmitter:
    def __init__(self): self._listeners: dict[str, list[Callable]] = {}
    def on(self, event: str, cb: Callable):
        self._listeners.setdefault(event, []).append(cb); return self
    def off(self, event: str, cb: Callable):
        if event in self._listeners: self._listeners[event].remove(cb)
    def emit(self, event: str, *args, **kwargs):
        for cb in self._listeners.get(event, []):
            cb(*args, **kwargs)

class Generation(EventEmitter):
    def run(self, tokens):
        for t in tokens:
            self.emit("token", t)
        self.emit("complete", "".join(tokens))

gen = Generation()
gen.on("token", lambda t: print(t, end=""))                  # stream to console
gen.on("complete", lambda full: print(f"\n[done] {len(full)} chars"))
gen.run(["Hel", "lo ", "world"])
# Hello world
# [done] 11 chars

The same emitter powers agent-step callbacks — observers react to each step without the agent loop knowing them:

class AgentRun(EventEmitter):
    def run(self, steps):
        for i in range(steps):
            self.emit("step_end", step=i, action=f"tool_call_{i}")

run = AgentRun()
run.on("step_end", lambda **kw: print(f"step {kw['step']}: {kw['action']}"))
run.on("step_end", lambda **kw: print("  (traced to LangSmith)"))
run.run(3)

When to use: Decoupled reaction to events — training callbacks, UI events, pub/sub, domain events. Subscribers don't know about each other; the subject doesn't know subscriber details.

Verdict: ✅ Useful and common. Python keeps it light: a list of callbacks, no Observer interface required. For anything bigger than in-process callbacks, reach for a real event bus / message queue rather than hand-rolling.

•

20. State

IntuitionstateReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: An object behaves differently depending on which state it's in, and each state knows the legal transitions out of itself. Like a traffic light: green's only move is to amber, amber's only move is to red. Instead of a sprawling if status == ... everywhere, each state owns its own rules.

Real-world: An agent-task or generation-job state machine: queued → running → awaiting_tool → done (or → failed), where the allowed actions differ per state.

Without the pattern — a sprawling conditional on a status string, repeated wherever behavior depends on state:

if   task.status == "queued":   task.status = "running"
elif task.status == "running":  task.status = "awaiting_tool"   # grows forever
elif task.status == "awaiting_tool": task.status = "done"

With the pattern — each state object knows its own transition:

task.advance()   # the current state decides the next one

From-scratch — an agent-task lifecycle, class-per-state (when each state has real behavior):

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class State(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def next(self, task): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def name(self) -> str: ...

class Queued(State):
    def next(self, task): task.state = Running()
    def name(self): return "QUEUED"
class Running(State):
    def next(self, task): task.state = AwaitingTool()
    def name(self): return "RUNNING"
class AwaitingTool(State):
    def next(self, task): task.state = Done()
    def name(self): return "AWAITING_TOOL"
class Done(State):
    def next(self, task): print("Task already done")
    def name(self): return "DONE"

class AgentTask:
    def __init__(self): self.state: State = Queued()
    def advance(self): self.state.next(self)
    @property
    def status(self): return self.state.name()

t = AgentTask()
for _ in range(4):
    print(t.status); t.advance()
# QUEUED / RUNNING / AWAITING_TOOL / DONE

Pythonic version — a transition table (best for simple FSMs):

from enum import Enum, auto

class S(Enum):
    QUEUED = auto(); RUNNING = auto(); DONE = auto()

TRANSITIONS = {S.QUEUED: {S.RUNNING}, S.RUNNING: {S.DONE}, S.DONE: set()}

def transition(current: S, target: S) -> S:
    if target not in TRANSITIONS[current]:
        raise ValueError(f"Illegal transition {current.name} → {target.name}")
    return target

When to use: State-dependent behavior with well-defined transitions — agent-task / generation-job lifecycles, streaming-connection state, multi-turn conversation phases (gathering → answering → awaiting-feedback).

Verdict: ✅ Useful for real FSMs — but use a transition table or match, not a class per state. For complex machines the transitions library is worth it. The class-per-state GoF form is overkill until each state has substantial unique behavior.

•

21. Strategy

IntuitionReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms and pick one at runtime. Because functions are first-class in Python, the simplest strategy is just a function you pass in. Like choosing which route app to follow on a trip — the car (the context) is the same; you swap the routing algorithm.

Real-world: Pluggable chunking (fixed-size vs. semantic vs. recursive), a reranking strategy, a retrieval strategy (dense vs. hybrid vs. BM25), or a retry-backoff strategy — all swapped at runtime.

Without the pattern — branch on a chunker name inside the method; adding one edits the method:

def split(self, text):
    if   self.kind == "fixed":     return ...
    elif self.kind == "paragraph": return ...   # grows every time you add a strategy

With the pattern — inject the algorithm (a plain function) and just call it:

index_document(text, chunker=by_paragraph)   # swap strategies without touching the indexer

From-scratch — strategy as a plain function (THE canonical example), here pluggable chunkers:

from typing import Callable

def fixed_size(text, size=20): return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), size)]
def by_paragraph(text):        return [p for p in text.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]

def index_document(text: str, chunker: Callable) -> list[str]:
    return chunker(text)   # the strategy is just a function passed in

doc = "para one.\n\npara two is a bit longer than the first one here."
print(index_document(doc, by_paragraph))            # ['para one.', 'para two is ...']
print(index_document(doc, lambda t: fixed_size(t, 15)))   # fixed 15-char chunks

Classic class-based form — only when strategies hold state (e.g. a reranker with config):

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Reranker(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def rank(self, query: str, docs: list[str]) -> list[str]: ...

class LexicalReranker(Reranker):
    def rank(self, query, docs):
        return sorted(docs, key=lambda d: query.lower() in d.lower(), reverse=True)
class LengthReranker(Reranker):
    def __init__(self, prefer_short=True): self.prefer_short = prefer_short
    def rank(self, query, docs):
        return sorted(docs, key=len, reverse=not self.prefer_short)

class Retriever:
    def __init__(self, reranker: Reranker): self.reranker = reranker
    def search(self, query, docs): return self.reranker.rank(query, docs)[:2]

docs = ["RAG combines retrieval and generation", "cats", "retrieval augments LLMs"]
print(Retriever(LexicalReranker()).search("retrieval", docs))
# ['RAG combines retrieval and generation', 'retrieval augments LLMs']

When to use: Swappable algorithms — loss functions, compression schemes, sorting/pricing/chunking rules. Prefer plain functions unless the strategy needs configuration/state.

Verdict: ❌ Dead as a class hierarchy — use first-class functions. This is the textbook case where Python erases a pattern: a Strategy is just a function (or callable) you pass as an argument. Building Strategy ABC + ConcreteStrategyA/B is the #1 "Java in Python" smell. If an interviewer asks for Strategy, pass a function.

•

22. Template Method

Intuitionorder is the contractReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: Fix the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, but leave specific steps blank for subclasses to fill in. Like a recipe template: "prep → cook → plate" is fixed, but each dish defines its own prep and cook. The order is the contract; subclasses only supply the steps.

Real-world: A base indexing pipeline with a fixed load → chunk → embed → index order where each source type (PDF, HTML, Notion) fills in the steps; or a base agent with overridable plan / act / reflect hooks around a fixed loop.

Without the pattern — every source type copy-pastes the same indexing skeleton:

def index_pdf(src):  raw = load(src); chunks = chunk(raw); index(embed(chunks))
def index_html(src): raw = load(src); chunks = chunk(raw); index(embed(chunks))   # duplicated flow

With the pattern — the base fixes the skeleton; subclasses fill only the steps that differ:

class PDFIndexer(IndexingPipeline): ...   # override load/embed/index only
PDFIndexer().run("manual.pdf")            # shared flow lives in one place

From-scratch — a document-indexing pipeline (load → chunk → embed → index):

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class IndexingPipeline(ABC):
    def run(self, source):                 # the template method (fixed skeleton — don't override)
        raw = self.load(source)
        chunks = self.chunk(raw)           # hook with a default
        vectors = self.embed(chunks)
        self.index(vectors)
        print(f"Done: indexed {len(vectors)} vectors")

    @abstractmethod
    def load(self, source): ...
    def chunk(self, raw):                  # overridable default: fixed 10-char chunks
        return [raw[i:i + 10] for i in range(0, len(raw), 10)]
    @abstractmethod
    def embed(self, chunks): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def index(self, vectors): ...

class PDFIndexer(IndexingPipeline):
    def load(self, source): return f"text extracted from {source}"
    def embed(self, chunks): return [[0.1] for _ in chunks]
    def index(self, vectors): print(f"  upserted {len(vectors)} vectors to Chroma")

PDFIndexer().run("manual.pdf")
#   upserted 3 vectors to Chroma
# Done: indexed 3 vectors

When to use: Several variants share the same overall flow but differ in individual steps — ETL pipelines, report generators, test fixtures.

Verdict: ⚠️ Works, but Strategy (composition) is often cleaner. Template Method uses inheritance to vary steps and fixes the algorithm's structure; injecting step-functions (Strategy) avoids rigid hierarchies. Use Template Method when the order is the contract and steps are tightly bound to the base. ABC + @abstractmethod is the right tool when you do.

•

23. Visitor

IntuitionvisitorReal-worldWithout the patternWith the patternWhen to use

Intuition: You have a fixed set of element types (shapes, AST nodes) and a growing set of operations over them. Rather than editing every element class each time you add an operation, put each operation in its own visitor object, and let elements "accept" a visitor that handles their type. Adding an operation = adding one visitor; no element edits.

Real-world: Walking the content blocks of a multimodal LLM message (text / image / tool-use) to render them, estimate token cost, or validate them — each new operation is one visitor, no edits to the block classes.

Without the pattern — every new operation forces you to edit every block class:

class TextBlock:
    def token_cost(self): ...
    def render(self): ...   # add a new op → touch TextBlock, ImageBlock, ToolUseBlock, …

With the pattern — one visitor adds an operation across all block types, no block edits:

block.accept(TokenCostVisitor())   # new operation = one new visitor class

From-scratch — content blocks of a multimodal message, classic double dispatch:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Block(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def accept(self, visitor): ...

class TextBlock(Block):
    def __init__(self, text): self.text = text
    def accept(self, v): return v.visit_text(self)
class ImageBlock(Block):
    def __init__(self, url): self.url = url
    def accept(self, v): return v.visit_image(self)
class ToolUseBlock(Block):
    def __init__(self, name, args): self.name, self.args = name, args
    def accept(self, v): return v.visit_tool(self)

class TokenCostVisitor:
    def visit_text(self, b):  return len(b.text) // 4            # ~4 chars per token
    def visit_image(self, b): return 85                          # flat image cost
    def visit_tool(self, b):  return 10 + len(str(b.args)) // 4
class RenderVisitor:
    def visit_text(self, b):  return b.text
    def visit_image(self, b): return f"[image: {b.url}]"
    def visit_tool(self, b):  return f"[tool {b.name}({b.args})]"

blocks = [TextBlock("Here is the chart"), ImageBlock("plot.png"), ToolUseBlock("search", {"q": "rag"})]
cost, render = TokenCostVisitor(), RenderVisitor()
print("tokens:", sum(b.accept(cost) for b in blocks))   # tokens: 4 + 85 + ...
print("render:", " ".join(b.accept(render) for b in blocks))
# render: Here is the chart [image: plot.png] [tool search({'q': 'rag'})]

Pythonic version — functools.singledispatch replaces the double-dispatch boilerplate:

from functools import singledispatch
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class TextNode:    content: str
@dataclass
class ImageNode:   url: str
@dataclass
class ToolUseNode: name: str

@singledispatch
def render(node) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError(f"No renderer for {type(node).__name__}")

@render.register
def _(node: TextNode):    return f"<p>{node.content}</p>"
@render.register
def _(node: ImageNode):   return f'<img src="{node.url}">'
@render.register
def _(node: ToolUseNode): return f"<tool>{node.name}</tool>"

When to use: A stable set of element classes but a growing set of operations over them (AST eval/print/optimize, report generators, geometry). Trade-off: adding a new element type forces updating every visitor.

Verdict: ⚠️ Use singledispatch, not the classic accept/visit boilerplate. The GoF Visitor exists to fake multiple dispatch in single-dispatch languages. Python gives you @singledispatch directly — same benefit, none of the ceremony. Niche, but clean when you need it.

Behavioral scorecard

PatternVerdictPython note
Chain of Responsibility✅list of callables; middleware
Command⚠️closure / partial unless undo/queue needed
Interpreter❌use ast / lark / pyparsing
Iterator❌generators (yield) are built in
Mediator✅multi-agent supervisor / orchestrator
Memento⚠️just serialize (dataclass/Pydantic dump)
Observer✅list of callbacks; event bus for scale
State✅transition table / match, not class-per-state
Strategy❌pass a function — the canonical example
Template Method⚠️ABC works; Strategy/composition often cleaner
Visitor⚠️functools.singledispatch

Part IV — Modern Application Patterns

Beyond the GoF set, these recur constantly in real services and GenAI systems.

•

M1. Dependency Injection

Intuitionhanded inWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: A component shouldn't build its own collaborators — they should be handed in from outside. Then in tests you can hand it a fake instead of the real thing. Like a coffee machine that takes whatever beans you pour in, rather than growing its own.

Without the pattern — a component builds its own collaborators, so you can't substitute them (e.g. a fake LLM in tests):

class RAGPipeline:
    def __init__(self):
        self.generator = OpenAIClient()   # hard-wired — every test hits the paid API

With the pattern — collaborators are passed in, so any implementation drops in:

RAGPipeline(retriever, FakeLLM(), evaluator)   # swap real ↔ mock, zero changes to RAGPipeline
class RAGPipeline:
    def __init__(self, retriever, generator, evaluator):   # injected
        self.retriever, self.generator, self.evaluator = retriever, generator, evaluator
    def run(self, query):
        docs = self.retriever.search(query)
        answer = self.generator.complete(query, docs)
        return self.evaluator.score(answer)
# In tests: RAGPipeline(FakeRetriever(), FakeLLM(), evaluator) — no real API calls, no token spend.

Verdict: ✅ The foundation of testable code. This isn't really a "pattern" so much as the default way to wire Python apps. FastAPI's Depends, pytest fixtures, and constructor injection all express it. For deep graphs, see the DI Container §M11.

•

M2. Specification (Composable Predicates)

IntuitionWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: Turn each retrieval/filter rule into a small object you can combine with &, |, ~ — like building a document filter out of reusable Lego bricks (relevant & recent & ~from_web) instead of one tangled boolean expression copy-pasted across every retriever.

Without the pattern — the post-retrieval filter is an ad-hoc boolean expression, duplicated and hard to recombine:

keep = [d for d in docs if d["score"] >= 0.8 and d["source"] != "web"]  # rule duplicated everywhere

With the pattern — each rule is a named object you combine with & | ~:

high_quality = ScoreAbove(0.8) & ~FromSource("web")
[d for d in docs if high_quality.is_satisfied(d)]
class Spec:
    def is_satisfied(self, item): raise NotImplementedError
    def __and__(self, o): return And(self, o)
    def __or__(self, o):  return Or(self, o)
    def __invert__(self): return Not(self)

class And(Spec):
    def __init__(self, *s): self.s = s
    def is_satisfied(self, i): return all(x.is_satisfied(i) for x in self.s)
class Or(Spec):
    def __init__(self, *s): self.s = s
    def is_satisfied(self, i): return any(x.is_satisfied(i) for x in self.s)
class Not(Spec):
    def __init__(self, s): self.s = s
    def is_satisfied(self, i): return not self.s.is_satisfied(i)

class ScoreAbove(Spec):
    def __init__(self, t): self.t = t
    def is_satisfied(self, d): return d["score"] >= self.t
class FromSource(Spec):
    def __init__(self, src): self.src = src
    def is_satisfied(self, d): return d["source"] == self.src

docs = [{"id": 1, "score": 0.91, "source": "docs"},
        {"id": 2, "score": 0.40, "source": "web"},
        {"id": 3, "score": 0.88, "source": "web"}]
high_quality = ScoreAbove(0.8) & ~FromSource("web")   # keep strong, non-web hits
print([d["id"] for d in docs if high_quality.is_satisfied(d)])   # [1]

Verdict: ✅ Clean when rules genuinely recombine. Operator overloading makes it read naturally. For one-off filters, a plain comprehension is simpler. Contrast with Interpreter §15: Specification combines predicates via & | ~; Interpreter parses an explicit grammar from text.

•

M3. Object Pool

IntuitionpoolWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: Some objects (authenticated LLM API sessions, embedding-server connections) are expensive to set up, so keep a pool of ready-made ones — borrow when you need one, return it when done, instead of building and tearing down each time. Like a tool-hire shop: rent a drill, return it, it's cleaned and re-shelved for the next person.

Without the pattern — build and tear down an expensive client session on every single request:

session = open_llm_session()   # costly auth handshake every time
...; session.close()           # discarded, rebuilt on the next call

With the pattern — borrow from and return to a pool of reusable sessions:

session = pool.acquire(); ...; pool.release(session)   # reused, not rebuilt
import threading

class Pool:
    def __init__(self, factory, max_size=3):
        self._factory, self._max = factory, max_size
        self._free, self._in_use = [], set()
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
    def acquire(self):
        with self._lock:
            if self._free:                      obj = self._free.pop()
            elif len(self._in_use) < self._max: obj = self._factory()
            else: raise RuntimeError("pool exhausted")
            self._in_use.add(id(obj)); return obj
    def release(self, obj):
        with self._lock:
            self._in_use.discard(id(obj)); self._free.append(obj)

# factory builds an authenticated LLM API session (expensive handshake)
pool = Pool(lambda: {"session": "llm-client"}, max_size=5)

Verdict: ⚠️ Use a library, don't hand-roll. Real pooling (SQLAlchemy's engine pool, concurrent.futures thread pools, HTTP connection pools) handles timeouts, health checks, and overflow. Build your own only for genuinely custom resources.

•

M4. Repository (+ Unit of Work)

IntuitionUnit of WorkWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: Hide where data lives behind a collection-like object — repo.find_by_id(1), repo.save(doc) — so your RAG/agent logic never touches the vector-DB SDK. Swap a real store for an in-memory dict in tests with zero changes to the logic. Unit of Work adds: batch a set of changes and commit (or roll back) them together, atomically.

Without the pattern — business code talks to the vector DB directly, coupling logic to the driver:

client.query(collection="docs", vector=v, top_k=5)   # storage details leak into domain logic

With the pattern — a collection-like interface hides storage; swap a real store for in-memory in tests:

repo.find_by_id(id)   # business code never sees the vector-DB SDK
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class DocumentRepository(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def find_by_id(self, id): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, doc): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def search(self, **criteria): ...

class InMemoryDocumentRepository(DocumentRepository):
    def __init__(self): self._store, self._next_id = {}, 1
    def find_by_id(self, id):  return self._store.get(id)
    def find_all(self):        return list(self._store.values())
    def save(self, doc):
        if "id" not in doc:
            doc["id"] = self._next_id; self._next_id += 1
        self._store[doc["id"]] = doc
        return doc
    def delete(self, id):      return self._store.pop(id, None)
    def search(self, **criteria):
        return [d for d in self._store.values()
                if all(d.get(k) == v for k, v in criteria.items())]

repo = InMemoryDocumentRepository()
repo.save({"title": "RAG guide", "source": "docs"})
repo.save({"title": "Agents 101", "source": "blog"})
repo.save({"title": "Embeddings FAQ", "source": "docs"})
print(repo.search(source="docs"))   # the two "docs" entries
print(repo.find_by_id(1))           # {'title': 'RAG guide', 'source': 'docs', 'id': 1}

Unit of Work — batch inserts/updates/deletes into one atomic commit():

class UnitOfWork:
    def __init__(self): self.new, self.dirty, self.removed = [], [], []
    def register_new(self, e):     self.new.append(e)
    def register_dirty(self, e):
        if e not in self.dirty: self.dirty.append(e)
    def register_removed(self, e): self.removed.append(e)
    def commit(self):
        for e in self.new:     print(f"  INSERT: {e}")
        for e in self.dirty:   print(f"  UPDATE: {e}")
        for e in self.removed: print(f"  DELETE: {e}")
        self.new.clear(); self.dirty.clear(); self.removed.clear()
    def rollback(self):
        self.new.clear(); self.dirty.clear(); self.removed.clear()
        print("  ROLLBACK")

Verdict: ✅ Worth it for testable business logic. Decouples the domain from the database (swap real ↔ in-memory in tests). Unit of Work adds transactional batching so a set of changes commits or rolls back together. Note that an ORM session (SQLAlchemy) is already a Unit of Work.

•

M5. Circuit Breaker

IntuitionWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: If a downstream service is failing, stop hammering it — "trip the breaker" and fail fast for a while, then cautiously test if it has recovered. Exactly like the electrical breaker in your house: after a fault it cuts the circuit so the fault can't cascade.

Without the pattern — you keep calling a dead LLM API on every request, piling up timeouts and cascading the failure:

return openai_client.complete(prompt)   # hammers a provider that's already returning 503s

With the pattern — after N failures the breaker opens and fails fast, then probes for recovery:

cb.call(lambda: openai_client.complete(prompt))   # blocks calls while OPEN, retries when likely healthy
import time
from enum import Enum

class BreakerState(Enum):
    CLOSED = "closed"; OPEN = "open"; HALF_OPEN = "half_open"

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.state = BreakerState.CLOSED
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.last_failure_time = None

    def call(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        if self.state == BreakerState.OPEN:
            if time.time() - self.last_failure_time > self.recovery_timeout:
                self.state = BreakerState.HALF_OPEN     # probe recovery
            else:
                raise Exception("Circuit is OPEN — request blocked")
        try:
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            self._on_success(); return result
        except Exception:
            self._on_failure(); raise

    def _on_success(self):
        self.failure_count = 0; self.state = BreakerState.CLOSED
    def _on_failure(self):
        self.failure_count += 1; self.last_failure_time = time.time()
        if self.failure_count >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.state = BreakerState.OPEN
            print(f"Circuit OPENED after {self.failure_count} failures")

cb = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=5)
def call_llm(): raise ConnectionError("LLM API 503")
for i in range(5):
    try: cb.call(call_llm)
    except Exception as e: print(f"Call {i+1}: {e} (state={cb.state.value})")

Verdict: ✅ Essential for resilient distributed systems — but use a library. pybreaker, tenacity (retry + backoff), or your service mesh implement this with metrics and half-open probing. The breaker prevents cascading failures and gives the dependency time to recover. Know the mechanism; configure a battle-tested one.

•

M6. Pipeline (Pipes & Filters)

IntuitionWithout the patternWith the patternboldevery

Intuition: Break a transformation into independent steps where each step's output feeds the next — a conveyor belt. Each step is a simple function; the pipeline composes them, and overloading __or__ gives a readable pipeline | step | step syntax.

Without the pattern — one monolithic function fuses every step, making it hard to reorder or reuse:

def prep(t):
    return [t[i:i+20] for i in range(0, len(t.strip().lower().replace("#", "")), 20)]  # welded together

With the pattern — independent steps composed in order, each swappable on its own:

pipeline | clean | strip_markdown | chunk
pipeline.execute(raw_doc)
class Pipeline:
    def __init__(self): self.steps = []
    def add(self, step): self.steps.append(step); return self
    def execute(self, data):
        result = data
        for step in self.steps:
            result = step(result)
        return result
    def __or__(self, step):          # enable: pipeline | step | step
        self.add(step); return self

def clean(t):          return t.strip().lower()
def strip_markdown(t): return t.replace("#", "").replace("*", "")
def chunk(t):          return [t[i:i + 20] for i in range(0, len(t), 20)]

pipeline = Pipeline()
pipeline | clean | strip_markdown | chunk      # RAG preprocessing for indexing
print(pipeline.execute("  # Heading with **bold** text to embed  "))
# ['heading with bold te', 'xt to embed']

Verdict: ✅ Clean for data/text transformation flows. ETL, ML preprocessing, request processing. Contrast with Chain of Responsibility §13: a pipeline runs every step in order and transforms data; CoR stops at the first handler that handles the request.

•

M7. Saga (Distributed Transactions)

Intuitioncompensating actionWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: You can't wrap calls across many microservices in a single database transaction, so instead give each step a compensating action (its "undo"). If a later step fails, you run the undos for the completed steps in reverse — like un-booking a flight and un-charging a card after the hotel booking fails.

Without the pattern — a partial failure leaves the index half-updated with no clean way back:

embed_chunks(); upsert_vectors(); update_metadata_db()   # if metadata write fails, orphan vectors remain

With the pattern — each step has a compensating action; a failure rolls completed steps back in reverse:

saga.run({})   # metadata write fails → delete vectors → drop embeddings, automatically
class SagaStep:
    def __init__(self, name, execute_fn, compensate_fn):
        self.name, self.execute, self.compensate = name, execute_fn, compensate_fn

class Saga:
    def __init__(self): self.steps, self.completed = [], []
    def add_step(self, name, execute_fn, compensate_fn):
        self.steps.append(SagaStep(name, execute_fn, compensate_fn)); return self
    def run(self, context):
        for step in self.steps:
            try:
                print(f"  Executing: {step.name}")
                step.execute(context); self.completed.append(step)
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"  FAILED: {step.name} — {e}")
                self._compensate(context); return False
        return True
    def _compensate(self, context):
        print("  Rolling back...")
        for step in reversed(self.completed):       # reverse order
            try:
                print(f"  Compensating: {step.name}"); step.compensate(context)
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"  Compensation failed: {step.name} — {e}")

saga = (Saga()
    .add_step("Embed chunks",
              lambda c: c.update({"vectors": [[0.1], [0.2]]}),
              lambda c: print("    Dropped embeddings"))
    .add_step("Upsert to vector DB",
              lambda c: c.update({"upserted": True}),
              lambda c: print("    Deleted vectors from store"))
    .add_step("Update metadata DB",
              lambda c: (_ for _ in ()).throw(Exception("metadata write failed")),
              lambda c: print("    Reverted metadata")))
ok = saga.run({})
print(f"Indexing {'succeeded' if ok else 'failed with rollback'}")

Verdict: ✅ The standard answer for cross-service consistency — but it's hard. Use it when a single ACID transaction is impossible. Each local step commits independently; failures trigger compensating transactions. In production, an orchestrator (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) manages the state and retries.

•

M8. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

IntuitionwritereadWithout the patternWith the patterneventually consistent

Intuition: Split the write side (commands that change state, recorded as events) from the read side (a query model tuned for fast reads). One model strained to do both well does neither; separating them lets each scale and optimize independently.

Without the pattern — one model serves both writes and complex reads, so neither is optimal:

db.execute("INSERT INTO messages ...")     # same schema strained for write integrity
db.execute("SELECT ... JOIN ... GROUP")    # and for fast transcript / analytics reads

With the pattern — a write model records events; a separate read model is tuned for queries:

write.send_message("c1", "user", "What is RAG?")
for e in write.events: read.apply(e)      # project onto a read model scaled independently
class Event:
    def __init__(self, type, data): self.type, self.data = type, data

class WriteModel:                                # command side: append chat events
    def __init__(self): self.events = []
    def send_message(self, conv, role, text):
        e = Event("MESSAGE_SENT", {"conv": conv, "role": role, "text": text})
        self.events.append(e); return e

class ReadModel:                                 # query side: a transcript view per conversation
    def __init__(self): self.conversations = {}
    def apply(self, event):
        if event.type == "MESSAGE_SENT":
            d = event.data
            self.conversations.setdefault(d["conv"], []).append((d["role"], d["text"]))
    def transcript(self, conv): return self.conversations.get(conv, [])

write, read = WriteModel(), ReadModel()
write.send_message("c1", "user", "What is RAG?")
write.send_message("c1", "assistant", "Retrieval-augmented generation.")
for event in write.events: read.apply(event)     # project events onto the read model
print(read.transcript("c1"))
# [('user', 'What is RAG?'), ('assistant', 'Retrieval-augmented generation.')]

Verdict: ⚠️ Powerful but heavy — only when read/write shapes truly diverge. Justified when read and write workloads have very different scaling needs, or you want a command audit trail. Often paired with Event Sourcing. Trade-off: the read model is eventually consistent with the write side. Don't reach for it in a CRUD app.

•

M9. Event Sourcing

Intuitionappend-only log of eventsWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: Instead of storing the current value and overwriting history, store an append-only log of events ("granted 10k tokens", "spent 1.5k on a call") and derive the current state by replaying them. You get a full audit trail and time-travel for free — like an itemized usage bill, not just a remaining balance.

Without the pattern — you store only the current value, overwriting history (no audit, no per-call attribution):

budget.remaining -= 1500   # which prompt spent it? gone forever

With the pattern — you append immutable events and derive state by replaying them:

budget.spend(1500)                          # records a SPENT event (with the call that caused it)
TokenBudget("team-A", store).rebuild()      # full history → reconstruct usage at any point
from datetime import datetime

class EventStore:
    def __init__(self): self.events = []
    def append(self, account_id, event_type, data):
        e = {"id": len(self.events) + 1, "account_id": account_id,
             "type": event_type, "data": data,
             "timestamp": datetime.now().isoformat()}
        self.events.append(e); return e
    def get_events(self, account_id):
        return [e for e in self.events if e["account_id"] == account_id]

class TokenBudget:
    def __init__(self, account_id, store: EventStore):
        self.id, self.store, self.remaining = account_id, store, 0
    def grant(self, tokens):
        self.store.append(self.id, "GRANTED", {"tokens": tokens})
        self.remaining += tokens
    def spend(self, tokens):
        if tokens > self.remaining: raise ValueError("Insufficient token budget")
        self.store.append(self.id, "SPENT", {"tokens": tokens})
        self.remaining -= tokens
    def rebuild(self):                       # derive state from the log
        self.remaining = 0
        for e in self.store.get_events(self.id):
            if e["type"] == "GRANTED":   self.remaining += e["data"]["tokens"]
            elif e["type"] == "SPENT":   self.remaining -= e["data"]["tokens"]
        return self.remaining

store = EventStore()
budget = TokenBudget("team-A", store)
budget.grant(10000); budget.spend(1500); budget.spend(2500)
print(budget.remaining)                             # 6000
print(TokenBudget("team-A", store).rebuild())       # 6000 (rebuilt from the event log)

Verdict: ⚠️ Strong audit/time-travel, real operational cost. Use it when you need a complete history, the ability to reconstruct past state, or to project the same events into multiple read models (pairs naturally with CQRS). Cost: replay/snapshot management and schema-evolution of old events. Overkill for most CRUD.

•

M10. Plugin System

IntuitionregisteringWithout the patternWith the pattern

Intuition: Let third parties extend your app by registering components against a known interface, discovered and invoked dynamically — without anyone editing the core. Like power sockets: the appliance maker doesn't touch your house wiring; they just build to the plug standard.

Without the pattern — adding a tool means editing the agent's if/elif dispatch:

if   name == "search": return web_search(arg)
elif name == "calc":   return str(eval(arg))   # the agent core must change for every new tool

With the pattern — tools register against an interface; the agent core stays untouched:

registry.register(SearchTool())
registry.call("search", "RAG")   # new tools added without editing the agent loop
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Tool(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def name(self): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def run(self, arg): ...

class SearchTool(Tool):
    def name(self): return "search"
    def run(self, arg): return f"results for {arg!r}"
class CalculatorTool(Tool):
    def name(self): return "calc"
    def run(self, arg): return f"= {eval(arg)}"      # demo only — never eval untrusted input
class SummarizeTool(Tool):
    def name(self): return "summarize"
    def run(self, arg): return f"summary of {len(arg)} chars"

class ToolRegistry:
    def __init__(self): self._tools = {}
    def register(self, tool: Tool):
        self._tools[tool.name()] = tool
    def call(self, name, arg):
        if name not in self._tools:
            raise ValueError(f"Tool '{name}' not found")
        return self._tools[name].run(arg)
    def list_tools(self): return list(self._tools)

registry = ToolRegistry()
for t in (SearchTool(), CalculatorTool(), SummarizeTool()): registry.register(t)
print(registry.list_tools())          # ['search', 'calc', 'summarize']
print(registry.call("search", "RAG")) # results for 'RAG'
print(registry.call("calc", "2+3*4")) # = 14

Verdict: ✅ The backbone of extensible apps. Editors, build tools, ML frameworks (custom layers/callbacks), CMSs. Combine with the Factory registry §2, importlib for runtime discovery, and Python entry_points for installable plugins. This is just the Factory registry plus a known interface.

•

M11. Dependency Injection Container

IntuitioncontainerWithout the patternWith the patternModern application patternsRule of thumb

Intuition: When the dependency graph gets deep (service needs a DB, which needs a logger, …), wiring it by hand everywhere is tedious and repetitive. A container maps names → factories, resolves the whole graph recursively from one resolve("user_service"), and can cache singletons — automating the manual DI of §M1.

Without the pattern — you wire the whole dependency graph by hand at every entry point:

emb = Embedder(); store = VectorStore(emb); rag = RAGService(store, emb)   # manual, repeated everywhere

With the pattern — a container resolves the graph (and caches singletons) from a name:

rag = container.resolve("rag")   # embedder + store wired automatically
class Container:
    def __init__(self):
        self._factories = {}
        self._singletons = {}    # names registered as singletons
        self._instances = {}     # cached singleton instances

    def register(self, name, factory, singleton=False):
        self._factories[name] = factory
        if singleton: self._singletons[name] = True

    def resolve(self, name):
        if name in self._instances:          # return cached singleton
            return self._instances[name]
        factory = self._factories.get(name)
        if not factory:
            raise ValueError(f"'{name}' not registered")
        instance = factory(self)             # factory may resolve its own deps
        if name in self._singletons:
            self._instances[name] = instance
        return instance

class Embedder:
    def embed(self, text): return [0.1, 0.2]
class VectorStore:
    def __init__(self, embedder): self.embedder = embedder
    def search(self, q): return ["doc1", "doc2"]          # uses self.embedder under the hood
class RAGService:
    def __init__(self, store, embedder): self.store, self.embedder = store, embedder
    def answer(self, q): return f"answer using {self.store.search(q)}"

c = Container()
c.register("embedder", lambda c: Embedder(), singleton=True)
c.register("store",    lambda c: VectorStore(c.resolve("embedder")), singleton=True)
c.register("rag",      lambda c: RAGService(c.resolve("store"), c.resolve("embedder")))
print(c.resolve("rag").answer("What is RAG?"))   # wires the whole graph
# answer using ['doc1', 'doc2']

Verdict: ⚠️ Only for large apps with deep graphs. The container resolves transitive dependencies and manages lifetimes (singleton vs per-resolve). For small apps, plain constructor injection (§M1) is simpler; FastAPI's Depends covers most web needs without a separate container.

The 23 GoF patterns, their verdict in Python, and what to actually reach for:

#PatternCategoryVerdictWhat to do in Python

3Abstract FactoryCreational⚠️Protocol + assembler
