Modern application patterns: Dependency Injection ✅ · Specification ✅ · Object Pool ⚠️ (use a library) · Repository + Unit of Work ✅ · Circuit Breaker ✅ (use a library) · Pipeline ✅ · Saga ✅ (hard) · CQRS ⚠️ · Event Sourcing ⚠️ · Plugin System ✅ · DI Container ⚠️.

Pattern Selection Cheat Sheet

Creational
  Factory           Pick a concrete class from a key/config (registry dict)
  Abstract Factory  Create consistent families of related objects
  Builder           Assemble a complex object step by step (fluent .build())
  Singleton         One shared instance (prefer a module / DI)
  Prototype         Clone configured templates (copy.deepcopy)

Structural
  Adapter           Make a mismatched interface fit the expected one
  Decorator (wrap)  Add concerns (log/cache/encrypt) by wrapping; stackable
  Facade            One simple entry point over a complex subsystem
  Proxy             Control access: caching, lazy load, permissions
  Composite         Treat leaves and trees uniformly (recursive structures)
  Bridge            Vary abstraction and implementation independently
  Flyweight         Share immutable intrinsic state across many objects

Behavioral
  Observer          Notify many subscribers on state change (callbacks)
  Strategy          Swap interchangeable algorithms (just pass a function)
  Command           Encapsulate actions for queue/undo/redo
  Iterator          Custom/lazy traversal (use generators)
  State             Behavior changes with state; explicit transitions
  Template Method   Fix the algorithm skeleton, override the steps
  Chain of Resp.    Pass requests down a pipeline of handlers (middleware)
  Mediator          Centralize many-to-many communication in a hub
  Visitor           Add operations over a fixed element set (double dispatch)
  Memento           Snapshot/restore state for undo without breaking encapsulation
  Interpreter       Evaluate sentences of a small grammar via an AST

Modern / Application
  Dependency Inj.   Pass collaborators in for testable, swappable code
  Specification     Composable business rules via & | ~
  Object Pool       Reuse expensive resources (connections, threads)
  Repository        Collection-like API over storage (+ Unit of Work)
  Circuit Breaker   Fail fast on a failing dependency; auto-recover
  Pipeline          Chain ordered transforms (pipes & filters)
  Saga              Distributed txn via per-step compensating actions
  CQRS              Split write (commands/events) from read (query model)
  Event Sourcing    Persist events; rebuild state by replaying them
  Plugin System     Register extensions against a known interface
  DI Container      Auto-resolve dependency graphs + singletons

Rule of thumb: reach for the lightest Python idiom first (a function for Strategy/Command, a generator for Iterator, a dict for Factory, a module for Singleton). Promote to a full class hierarchy only when you need polymorphism, shared state, or an explicit, documented contract.

The one-liner for interviews

"I know the catalog, but in Python I lean on language features first — functions for Strategy/Command, generators for Iterator, @ for Decorator, modules for Singleton, deepcopy/replace for Prototype. I reach for an explicit pattern only when the language doesn't already give it to me cleanly — Adapter, Facade, Composite, Observer, State, and the Factory registry being the ones that actually earn their keep."

That sentence is the senior signal: it shows you know when not to reach for a pattern.

SOLID Principles12 sections

SOLID Principles — Master Reference

What this is: The five object-oriented design principles every senior Python / AI engineer is expected to apply, not just recite. SOLID is the layer beneath the design patterns — patterns are concrete recipes; SOLID is the set of forces those recipes are trying to balance. Get SOLID right and most patterns fall out naturally.

Coined by: Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob"). The acronym was assembled later by Michael Feathers.

Every worked example is GenAI. The code uses LLM / RAG / agent / embedding scenarios — providers, vector stores, tools, token budgets. The one-line metaphors are teaching aids only.

How each principle is explained: 1. One-liner — the principle in a single sentence. 2. Intuition — the idea in plain words, with a metaphor. 3. The smell it removes — what bad code looks like before. 4. From-scratch code — Bad vs Good, runnable, GenAI-flavoured. 5. The test — a quick heuristic to know if you're violating it. 6. When NOT to apply it — because over-applying SOLID is its own anti-pattern.

The meta-lesson (read twice): SOLID is not five rules to maximise. It's a vocabulary for talking about change — what is likely to change, and have I isolated it so the change stays small? A junior memorises the letters. A senior knows when applying a letter adds an abstraction nobody needs yet (YAGNI). Both halves of that judgement are what interviewers probe.

•

0. The 30-Second Summary

one reason to changeextensionmodificationanywhereabstractionsMnemonic for what each protects
LetterNameOne-line ruleSmell it kills
SSingle ResponsibilityA class should have one reason to change.God classes; "and" in the class description.
OOpen/ClosedOpen for extension, closed for modification.A growing if/elif you edit for every new case.
LLiskov SubstitutionSubtypes must be usable anywhere the base type is, without surprises.Overrides that throw, weaken outputs, or break promises.
IInterface SegregationDon't force clients to depend on methods they don't use.Fat interfaces; raise NotImplementedError stubs.
DDependency InversionDepend on abstractions, not concretions. High-level policy shouldn't import low-level detail.OpenAI() hard-coded deep inside business logic.

Mnemonic for what each protects: S = clarity, O = extensibility, L = substitutability, I = minimal contracts, D = testability/swappability.

•

1. S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

One-linerIntuitionThe smellandThe testWhen NOT to apply it

One-liner: A class (or module, or function) should have one, and only one, reason to change.

Intuition: "Reason to change" means one stakeholder / one axis of change. A Swiss-army-knife class that parses input, calls an LLM, formats Markdown, and writes to a database has four bosses — the prompt team, the provider team, the docs team, and the DB team can each force you to edit it. Every edit risks breaking the other three. Split it so each boss touches their own file.

Metaphor: a restaurant doesn't make the chef also take reservations, wash dishes, and do the accounting. One role, one reason to get reassigned.

The smell: you describe the class with the word "and" ("it summarises the document and saves it and emails it"). Or a single class file keeps getting touched in unrelated PRs.

Before — one class, four reasons to change

# ❌ SRP violation: a "RAG service" that does everything
class RagService:
    def answer(self, question: str) -> str:
        # 1. retrieval logic (changes when we swap vector DB)
        chunks = self._search_pinecone(question)
        # 2. prompt construction (changes when prompt team iterates)
        prompt = f"Context:\n{chunks}\n\nQ: {question}\nA:"
        # 3. provider call (changes when we move OpenAI -> Anthropic)
        answer = self._call_openai(prompt)
        # 4. persistence (changes when analytics wants a new schema)
        self._log_to_postgres(question, answer)
        return answer
    # ...four private methods, four teams editing one file, merge hell.

After — each responsibility isolated

# ✅ Each collaborator has exactly one reason to change.
class Retriever:
    def search(self, query: str) -> list[str]: ...

class PromptBuilder:
    def build(self, question: str, chunks: list[str]) -> str: ...

class LLMClient:
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class QALogger:
    def record(self, question: str, answer: str) -> None: ...

class RagPipeline:
    """Orchestrates — but owns no business logic itself."""
    def __init__(self, retriever, prompt_builder, llm, logger):
        self.retriever, self.prompt_builder = retriever, prompt_builder
        self.llm, self.logger = llm, logger

    def answer(self, question: str) -> str:
        chunks = self.retriever.search(question)
        prompt = self.prompt_builder.build(question, chunks)
        answer = self.llm.complete(prompt)
        self.logger.record(question, answer)
        return answer

Now the prompt team edits PromptBuilder, the infra team edits Retriever, and RagPipeline only changes if the steps themselves change.

The test: "How many distinct teams / future feature-requests would force me to open this file?" If more than one, you likely have more than one responsibility.

When NOT to apply it: don't shatter a 20-line script into seven classes. SRP earns its keep when responsibilities change at different rates or for different reasons — premature splitting just spreads one idea across files you must read together. Cohesion over ceremony.

•

2. O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

One-linerIntuitionThe smellwriting a new classThe testWhen NOT to apply it

One-liner: Software entities should be open for extension, closed for modification — add new behaviour without editing existing, tested code.

Intuition: the code you already shipped and tested is a liability to touch — every edit risks a regression. OCP says: design the extension point so new cases plug in from the outside. The classic tell of a violation is a type-switch (if provider == "openai": ... elif provider == "anthropic": ...) that you must crack open and edit for every new provider.

Metaphor: a power strip. You add a new device by plugging it in, not by rewiring the wall.

The smell: a growing if/elif/else (or match) on a "kind" field, where every new kind means editing the same function.

Before — edit the function for every new provider

# ❌ Every new provider forces a change to this tested method.
class Router:
    def embed(self, text: str, provider: str) -> list[float]:
        if provider == "openai":
            return openai_embed(text)
        elif provider == "cohere":
            return cohere_embed(text)
        elif provider == "voyage":          # <- had to reopen + retest this
            return voyage_embed(text)
        raise ValueError(provider)

After — closed to edits, open to new plug-ins

from typing import Protocol

class Embedder(Protocol):                 # the extension point (an abstraction)
    def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]: ...

class OpenAIEmbedder:
    def embed(self, text): return openai_embed(text)

class CohereEmbedder:
    def embed(self, text): return cohere_embed(text)

class VoyageEmbedder:                      # ✅ new provider = NEW file, zero edits
    def embed(self, text): return voyage_embed(text)

class Router:
    def __init__(self, embedder: Embedder):
        self._embedder = embedder          # closed: never edited for a new provider
    def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        return self._embedder.embed(text)

Adding Voyage meant writing a new class, not modifying Router. The Strategy and Factory patterns exist mostly to serve OCP.

The test: "To add the next variant, do I edit existing code or just add new code?" If you must edit, the entity isn't closed.

When NOT to apply it: you can't make code open to every axis of change — abstracting against changes that never come is speculative generality (YAGNI). Apply OCP on the axis that has already changed once or twice. The second elif is your signal; the first one is fine.

•

3. L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

One-linerIntuitionstrengthened the preconditionWeakenStrengthenPreserve invariants

One-liner: If S is a subtype of T, you must be able to substitute S anywhere T is expected without breaking the program's correctness.

Intuition: subclassing promises "I am a drop-in replacement." LSP is about honouring that promise behaviourally, not just syntactically. A subclass that throws where the parent succeeds, demands stricter inputs, or returns weaker outputs is a liar — code written against the parent will break when handed the child. It's the deepest and most-violated of the five.

Metaphor: a "rechargeable battery" is a valid substitute for a "battery." A "decorative battery-shaped candle" fits the slot but doesn't power the torch — it's not a subtype, even though it looks like one.

The classic trap (the contract, not the shape):

# ❌ LSP violation: the subclass narrows the parent's promise.
class LLMClient:
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        """Returns a completion for ANY non-empty prompt."""
        ...

class StrictModerationClient(LLMClient):
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        if contains_pii(prompt):
            raise ValueError("refusing prompt")   # parent never raised this!
        return super().complete(prompt)

Any function written to LLMClient's contract — "give me a string, get a string" — now crashes when secretly handed a StrictModerationClient. The subclass strengthened the precondition (it demands "no PII"), which LSP forbids.

The rules LSP actually encodes

A valid subtype may: - Weaken preconditions (accept more inputs) — never strengthen them. - Strengthen postconditions (promise more about outputs) — never weaken them. - Preserve invariants of the base type, and not throw new checked exceptions.

After — substitutable by construction

# ✅ Moderation is a SEPARATE concern, not a sneaky subtype.
class ModeratedLLM(LLMClient):
    """Still fulfils 'any prompt -> a string'. Refusal is a normal RESULT,
    not a broken contract."""
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        if contains_pii(prompt):
            return "[response withheld: prompt contained sensitive data]"
        return super().complete(prompt)

The canonical academic example: Square extending Rectangle. Rectangle promises set_width(w) leaves height unchanged. Square can't honour that (setting width must change height too), so Square is not a behavioural subtype of Rectangle — even though "a square is a rectangle" in maths. Prefer composition or a shared Shape abstraction.

The test: "Can I hand an instance of the subclass to old code written against the base — and would that code still be correct, with no isinstance checks?" If you find yourself writing if isinstance(x, SubType), LSP is already broken.

When NOT to worry about it: if you're not subclassing for substitutability (e.g. you use inheritance only for code reuse within a closed module and never pass children where parents are expected), the risk is lower — but composition is usually the cleaner fix anyway.

•

4. I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

One-linerIntuitionThe smellThe testRelationship to SRPinterfaces/contracts

One-liner: No client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Prefer many small, role-specific interfaces over one fat one.

Intuition: a fat interface couples unrelated clients together. If VectorStore declares search, insert, delete, reindex, snapshot, and restore, then a read-only query path is forced to depend on restore — and the day restore's signature changes, the query code recompiles/retests for no reason. Worse, an in-memory test double must stub six methods to use one.

Metaphor: a printer that's also a fax and a scanner. If all you want is to print, you still inherit the "out of fax toner" failure modes.

The smell: classes implementing an interface with bodies that raise NotImplementedError, or test mocks that stub a pile of methods nobody calls.

Before — one fat interface

# ❌ A read-only consumer must still depend on (and mock) write/admin methods.
class VectorStore(Protocol):
    def search(self, q: list[float], k: int) -> list[str]: ...
    def insert(self, id: str, vec: list[float]) -> None: ...
    def delete(self, id: str) -> None: ...
    def reindex(self) -> None: ...
    def snapshot(self, path: str) -> None: ...

class ReadOnlyCache(VectorStore):
    def search(self, q, k): ...
    def insert(self, *_):   raise NotImplementedError  # smell
    def delete(self, *_):   raise NotImplementedError  # smell
    def reindex(self):      raise NotImplementedError  # smell
    def snapshot(self, _):  raise NotImplementedError  # smell

After — split by role

# ✅ Each client depends only on the slice it needs.
class Searchable(Protocol):
    def search(self, q: list[float], k: int) -> list[str]: ...

class Writable(Protocol):
    def insert(self, id: str, vec: list[float]) -> None: ...
    def delete(self, id: str) -> None: ...

class Maintainable(Protocol):
    def reindex(self) -> None: ...
    def snapshot(self, path: str) -> None: ...

# The query path asks for the narrowest contract it can:
def rerank(store: Searchable, query: list[float]) -> list[str]:
    return store.search(query, k=20)

# A full store simply implements all three roles:
class PineconeStore(Searchable, Writable, Maintainable): ...
# A read-only cache implements ONLY Searchable — no fake stubs.
class ReadOnlyCache(Searchable): ...

The test: "Does any implementer of this interface have methods it has to fake?" and "Does any caller import an interface but use only one of its methods?" Either is an ISP smell.

Relationship to SRP: ISP is SRP applied to interfaces/contracts instead of classes. Same instinct — narrow, focused, one-reason-to-change — pointed at the boundary rather than the implementation.

When NOT to over-split: don't create a one-method interface for every method just to be pure. Split by the roles real clients actually request, not by every conceivable slice.

•

5. D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

One-linerboth should depend on abstractionsIntuitioninverts the arrowThe smelltestability

One-liner: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. And abstractions should not depend on details — details depend on abstractions.

Intuition: your business logic (the policy — "answer the user's question using retrieved context") is valuable and stable. The provider SDK (the detail — openai==1.x) is volatile and replaceable. If policy imports the detail directly, the volatile thing controls the stable thing — you can't test the policy without a network key, and swapping providers means surgery on business logic. DIP inverts the arrow: define an abstraction the policy owns, and make the detail conform to it.

Metaphor: a wall socket. Your lamp (high-level) doesn't solder itself to the power station (low-level); both agree on the plug shape (abstraction). Either side can change independently.

The smell: from openai import OpenAI near the top of your domain/business module; constructors that new up their own concrete collaborators.

Before — policy nailed to a detail

# ❌ The agent OWNS the concrete client. Can't test without a key; can't swap providers.
from openai import OpenAI

class SupportAgent:
    def __init__(self):
        self._client = OpenAI()          # hard dependency on a low-level detail
    def handle(self, msg: str) -> str:
        resp = self._client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": msg}])
        return resp.choices[0].message.content

After — depend on an abstraction the policy defines

from typing import Protocol

# The abstraction is OWNED by the high-level policy layer.
class ChatModel(Protocol):
    def reply(self, message: str) -> str: ...

class SupportAgent:                       # high-level policy
    def __init__(self, model: ChatModel): # injected, not constructed
        self._model = model
    def handle(self, msg: str) -> str:
        return self._model.reply(msg)

# Low-level details conform to the abstraction (they depend on IT, not vice-versa):
class OpenAIChat:
    def __init__(self): from openai import OpenAI; self._c = OpenAI()
    def reply(self, message): ...

class AnthropicChat:                       # swap with one line at the composition root
    def reply(self, message): ...

class FakeChat:                            # ✅ instant, offline, deterministic tests
    def reply(self, message): return "stubbed reply"

# Composition root (main.py) wires concretes to policy — the ONE place details live:
agent = SupportAgent(model=OpenAIChat())

DIP is what makes the Dependency Injection pattern possible, and it's the single biggest lever for testability — FakeChat lets you unit-test SupportAgent with no network, no key, no flakiness.

DIP ≠ DI. Dependency Inversion is the principle (depend on abstractions). Dependency **Injection is one technique for achieving it (pass collaborators in rather than constructing them). You can satisfy DIP without a DI framework — plain constructor arguments, as above, are enough.

The test: "Can I unit-test this class without touching the network, filesystem, or a real database?" If not, you're probably depending on a concretion you should have inverted.

When NOT to apply it: don't introduce an interface for a dependency that is genuinely stable and will never be swapped (the standard library's json, a pure helper). Inverting everything buries the code under one-implementation interfaces — abstraction with no payoff.

•

6. How the five fit together

localise changeDIPOCPLSPISPSRP

They're not five isolated rules; they reinforce each other around one goal — localise change:

        SRP  — one reason to change  ──┐  (split responsibilities so a change
        ISP  — one reason per contract ┤   touches one small place)
                                        │
        OCP  — extend without editing  ─┤  (add the new behaviour beside the old,
        DIP  — depend on abstractions  ─┘   plugged in through an abstraction)
                                        │
        LSP  — substitutes don't lie   ──── (so the plug-ins are actually safe
                                             to swap behind that abstraction)

A worked chain: DIP says depend on a ChatModel abstraction. OCP says a new provider should plug in without editing the agent — which the abstraction enables. LSP says every provider you plug in must honour ChatModel's contract (no surprise exceptions), or the swap isn't safe. ISP says ChatModel should stay narrow so providers don't fake methods. SRP says the agent orchestrates and the provider talks to the API — separate reasons to change. Pull one thread and the others follow.

•

7. SOLID ↔ Design Patterns map

OCPDIPSRPISPLSP

Patterns are the machinery that delivers a SOLID principle. (See the full catalogue in Design_Patterns_Master.md.)

PrinciplePatterns that exist largely to serve it
OCPStrategy, Template Method, Decorator, Factory Method, Abstract Factory — all add behaviour without editing the core.
DIPDependency Injection, Abstract Factory, Service Locator — invert who depends on whom.
SRPFacade (one front for a subsystem), Mediator, Command (one action per object).
ISPAdapter (expose only the slice a client needs), Role interfaces.
LSPUnderpins every polymorphic pattern — if substitution lies, Strategy/State/Template all break.

The senior insight: patterns without SOLID are cargo-culting. If you reach for Strategy but your strategies aren't substitutable (LSP) or your client still edits a switch statement (OCP), the pattern bought you nothing but indirection.

•

8. The Pythonic caveat

Duck typing softens ISP & DIPwithoutintentceremony

SOLID was articulated for statically-typed OO languages (C++, Java). Python changes the cost-benefit, not the goal:

  • Duck typing softens ISP & DIP. You often don't need a declared interface — any object with a reply method is a ChatModel. typing.Protocol gives you the abstraction's documentation and mypy checking without forcing inheritance (structural, not nominal). Use Protocols at real seams; don't ceremonially wrap every class.
  • First-class functions collapse some OCP/Strategy cases. Where Java needs a Strategy interface with one method, Python can pass a function. A Callable[[str], list[float]] is your Embedder.
  • The principles still bite where it counts: SRP (god classes hurt in any language), LSP (a lying duck-typed substitute is worse — no compiler catches it), and DIP for testability (injecting a fake is the whole game in unit tests).

Rule of thumb: keep the intent of every letter; spend the ceremony (explicit ABCs/Protocols) only at boundaries that actually change or get mocked.

•

9. Cohesion & Coupling (the why beneath SOLID)

high cohesionlow couplingCohesionHighCouplingLow

Every SOLID letter is, ultimately, a move toward high cohesion and low coupling — the two metrics that predict whether a codebase is pleasant or painful to change.

  • Cohesion = how strongly the things inside a module belong together. High is good: a PromptBuilder whose every method is about building prompts. SRP and ISP push cohesion up.
  • Coupling = how much one module must know about another's internals. Low is good: SupportAgent knowing only ChatModel.reply, not OpenAI's SDK shape. DIP, OCP, and LSP push coupling down.
Low coupling (good)High coupling (bad)
High cohesion (good)🟢 The goal: small, focused, swappable modules🟡 Tidy modules wired too tightly
Low cohesion (bad)🟡 Loose but each module is a grab-bag🔴 The "big ball of mud" — change anything, break everything

If you ever forget the five letters, remember the two words: cohere, decouple. SOLID is just five concrete tactics for getting there.

•

10. Interview drill

Q1. State SOLID in one breathLSPclass'sinterface'sQ4. DIP vs Dependency Injection?principle

Q1. State SOLID in one breath.

S — one reason to change; O — extend without editing; L — subtypes substitute safely; I — small focused interfaces; D — depend on abstractions.

Q2. Which is the most violated, and give a real example.

LSP. It's behavioural, so no compiler catches it. Classic: Square(Rectangle) — set_width can't keep its promise to leave height untouched. Or a subclass that raises where the parent returns. The fix is usually composition or a shared abstraction, not deeper inheritance.

Q3. SRP vs ISP — aren't they the same?

Same instinct ("one reason to change"), different target. SRP is about a class's responsibilities; ISP is about an interface's surface so clients aren't forced to depend on unused methods.

Q4. DIP vs Dependency Injection?

DIP is the principle — high-level code depends on abstractions. DI is one technique to achieve it — pass collaborators in instead of constructing them. Constructor arguments satisfy DIP; you don't need a framework.

Q5. How does OCP relate to the Strategy pattern?

Strategy is OCP made concrete: behaviour lives behind an interface, so a new algorithm is a new class plugged in at the composition root — the consumer is never edited. The tell that you need it: a second elif on a "kind" field.

Q6. When does applying SOLID become a mistake?

When you abstract against change that hasn't happened (speculative generality / YAGNI). Every interface and indirection has a reading cost. Apply OCP/DIP on axes that have already changed once or twice; don't wrap a stable stdlib call in a Protocol just to be "pure."

Q7. Give a single GenAI example touching all five.

A RagPipeline (SRP: orchestrates, owns no logic) depends on a Retriever/LLMClient abstraction (DIP), so a new vector DB or provider plugs in without editing the pipeline (OCP); every provider honours the client contract — no surprise raises (LSP); and the read path asks only for Searchable, not a fat store interface (ISP).

•

If you remember nothing elseSee also
LetterPrincipleThe smell (before)The fix (after)Quick self-test
SSingle Responsibility"...and..." in the class description; one file in unrelated PRsSplit by reason-to-changeHow many teams force me to edit this?
OOpen/ClosedGrowing if/elif on a "kind" fieldStrategy / polymorphism behind an interfaceNew variant = new code, or edited code?
LLiskov SubstitutionOverride that raises, narrows input, or weakens output; isinstance checksComposition or shared abstraction; honour the contractCan old base-typed code use the child unchanged?

DDependency Inversionimport openai in business logic; self.x = Concrete()Inject an abstraction; wire concretes at the composition rootCan I unit-test this with no network?

If you remember nothing else: SOLID is five tactics for one strategy — make change cheap by keeping it local. High cohesion, low coupling. Everything else is detail.

1.1 pdb / ipdb — Command Reference

# Launch debugger
import pdb; pdb.set_trace()     # classic
import ipdb; ipdb.set_trace()   # ipdb (colored, tab-complete)
breakpoint()                    # Python 3.7+ (preferred)
CommandDescription
n (next)Execute next line (step over)
s (step)Step into function call
c (continue)Continue until next breakpoint
r (return)Continue until current function returns
l (list)Show source around current line
llShow full source of current function
p exprPrint expression value
pp exprPretty-print expression
w (where)Print stack trace
u (up)Move one frame up in call stack
d (down)Move one frame down in call stack
b NSet breakpoint at line N
b funcSet breakpoint at function entry
b file:NSet breakpoint in another file
cl NClear breakpoint number N
clClear all breakpoints
tbreak NTemporary breakpoint (auto-cleared after hit)
condition N exprBreak at N only if expr is truthy
commands NExecute commands when breakpoint N is hit
interactStart interactive Python shell in current frame
a (args)Print arguments of current function
!stmtExecute statement (useful when var shadows command)
q (quit)Abort program

1.4 Post-Mortem Debugging

# After an exception — inspect the crash state
import pdb

try:
    result = buggy_function()
except Exception:
    pdb.post_mortem()  # drops into debugger at exception point

# Or from command line:
# python -m pdb script.py   (auto post-mortem on crash)

# Global exception hook
import sys
def debug_hook(exc_type, exc_value, exc_tb):
    if exc_type is not KeyboardInterrupt:
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exception(exc_type, exc_value, exc_tb)
        pdb.post_mortem(exc_tb)

sys.excepthook = debug_hook

1.6 Profiling as Debugging

# cProfile — function-level
import cProfile
cProfile.run("train_epoch(model, dataloader)", sort="cumulative")

# As decorator
def profile(func):
    import cProfile, pstats, io
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        pr = cProfile.Profile()
        pr.enable()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        pr.disable()
        s = io.StringIO()
        pstats.Stats(pr, stream=s).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(20)
        print(s.getvalue())
        return result
    return wrapper

# line_profiler — line-by-line
# pip install line_profiler
# @profile  (decorator added by kernprof)
# kernprof -l -v script.py

# memory_profiler
# pip install memory_profiler
# @profile
# python -m memory_profiler script.py

# py-spy — sampling profiler (no code changes)
# pip install py-spy
# py-spy top --pid 12345
# py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python train.py

1.7 Debugging ML Training Loops

import torch

def debug_training(model, dataloader, optimizer):
    model.train()
    for batch_idx, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(dataloader):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(outputs, targets)

        # Debug: check for NaN/Inf
        if torch.isnan(loss) or torch.isinf(loss):
            print(f"Bad loss at batch {batch_idx}: {loss.item()}")
            print(f"Input range: [{inputs.min():.4f}, {inputs.max():.4f}]")
            print(f"Output range: [{outputs.min():.4f}, {outputs.max():.4f}]")
            breakpoint()

        loss.backward()

        # Debug: check gradient norms
        total_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        if total_norm > 100:
            print(f"Exploding gradients at batch {batch_idx}: norm={total_norm:.2f}")

        # Debug: detect dead neurons
        if batch_idx % 100 == 0:
            for name, param in model.named_parameters():
                if param.grad is not None:
                    if param.grad.abs().max() < 1e-8:
                        print(f"Vanishing gradient in {name}")

        optimizer.step()

2.2 Pickle Security — Critical Risk

# DANGER: pickle executes arbitrary code during deserialization
import pickle

class Exploit:
    def __reduce__(self):
        import os
        return (os.system, ("rm -rf / --no-preserve-root",))

# This payload runs the command when unpickled:
payload = pickle.dumps(Exploit())
pickle.loads(payload)  # EXECUTES THE COMMAND

# NEVER unpickle untrusted data (user uploads, network data, etc.)

Safe Alternatives

# For ML models
import safetensors  # pip install safetensors
from safetensors.torch import save_file, load_file
# save_file({"weight": tensor}, "model.safetensors")
# tensors = load_file("model.safetensors")

# For data exchange
import json                   # text, safe, slow for large data
import msgspec                # fast JSON/msgpack, safe
import numpy as np
np.save("data.npy", array)   # numpy native format, safe

# For config
import tomllib                # Python 3.11+, safe
import yaml                   # use yaml.safe_load(), NEVER yaml.load()
•

2.3 Input Validation Patterns

# SQL Injection prevention — ALWAYS use parameterized queries
import sqlite3

# WRONG
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{user_input}'"

# RIGHT
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (user_input,))

# SQLAlchemy
from sqlalchemy import text
result = session.execute(text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id"), {"id": user_id})

# subprocess — NEVER use shell=True with user input
import subprocess

# WRONG
subprocess.run(f"grep {user_input} file.txt", shell=True)

# RIGHT
subprocess.run(["grep", user_input, "file.txt"], shell=False)

# eval/exec — NEVER on user input
# WRONG: eval(user_expression)
# RIGHT: use ast.literal_eval() for safe evaluation of literals
import ast
data = ast.literal_eval("{'key': 'value'}")  # safe

2.6 Cryptographic Best Practices

import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets

# Hashing (NOT for passwords)
digest = hashlib.sha256(b"data").hexdigest()

# Password hashing — use dedicated libraries
# pip install bcrypt
import bcrypt
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(b"password", bcrypt.gensalt())
bcrypt.checkpw(b"password", hashed)  # True

# HMAC — verify message integrity
key = secrets.token_bytes(32)
mac = hmac.new(key, b"message", hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

# Timing-safe comparison (prevents timing attacks)
hmac.compare_digest(mac, received_mac)

# NEVER:
# - Use MD5/SHA1 for security (only checksums)
# - Roll your own crypto
# - Use random module for security (use secrets instead)
# - Hardcode keys/salts

3.1 structlog — Bound Loggers and Processors

import structlog

structlog.configure(
    processors=[
        structlog.contextvars.merge_contextvars,
        structlog.processors.add_log_level,
        structlog.processors.TimeStamper(fmt="iso"),
        structlog.processors.StackInfoRenderer(),
        structlog.processors.format_exc_info,
        structlog.processors.JSONRenderer(),   # JSON output
    ],
    wrapper_class=structlog.make_filtering_bound_logger(logging.INFO),
    context_class=dict,
    logger_factory=structlog.PrintLoggerFactory(),
)

log = structlog.get_logger()

# Bound loggers — carry context
log = log.bind(service="inference", version="2.1")
log.info("model_loaded", model="bert-base", load_time_ms=342)
# {"service": "inference", "version": "2.1", "event": "model_loaded",
#  "model": "bert-base", "load_time_ms": 342, "level": "info",
#  "timestamp": "2026-05-31T10:30:00Z"}

log.warning("high_latency", endpoint="/predict", latency_ms=2500)

3.2 Logging in Async Applications

import structlog
from structlog.contextvars import bind_contextvars, clear_contextvars

async def handle_request(request_id: str):
    clear_contextvars()
    bind_contextvars(request_id=request_id)

    log = structlog.get_logger()
    log.info("request_started")     # automatically includes request_id
    result = await process(request_id)
    log.info("request_completed")   # still has request_id
    return result

3.3 Correlation IDs for Distributed Systems

import uuid
from contextvars import ContextVar
import structlog

correlation_id: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("correlation_id", default="")

def add_correlation_id(logger, method_name, event_dict):
    cid = correlation_id.get()
    if cid:
        event_dict["correlation_id"] = cid
    return event_dict

structlog.configure(
    processors=[
        add_correlation_id,
        structlog.processors.JSONRenderer(),
    ]
)

# FastAPI middleware
from fastapi import Request
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

class CorrelationMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        cid = request.headers.get("X-Correlation-ID", str(uuid.uuid4()))
        correlation_id.set(cid)
        response = await call_next(request)
        response.headers["X-Correlation-ID"] = cid
        return response

3.5 Logging for ML Training

import structlog

log = structlog.get_logger()

def train_with_logging(model, dataloader, epochs):
    log.info("training_started", epochs=epochs, total_batches=len(dataloader))

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        for batch_idx, batch in enumerate(dataloader):
            loss = train_step(model, batch)
            epoch_loss += loss

            if batch_idx % 100 == 0:
                log.info("batch_update",
                    epoch=epoch, batch=batch_idx,
                    loss=round(loss, 4),
                    lr=optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"],
                    gpu_mem_mb=torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e6
                )

        avg_loss = epoch_loss / len(dataloader)
        val_metrics = evaluate(model)
        log.info("epoch_complete",
            epoch=epoch, train_loss=round(avg_loss, 4),
            val_loss=round(val_metrics["loss"], 4),
            val_acc=round(val_metrics["accuracy"], 4)
        )
Part 4: Python Internals
•

4.1 CPython Compilation Pipeline

Source Code (.py)
    ↓  tokenizer (Lib/tokenize.py)
Tokens
    ↓  parser (Grammar/python.gram → PEG parser)
AST (Abstract Syntax Tree)
    ↓  compiler (Python/compile.c)
Bytecode (Code Object)
    ↓  VM execution (Python/ceval.c)
Result

# Inspect each stage:
import tokenize, ast, dis, io

source = "x = [i**2 for i in range(10)]"

# 1. Tokens
tokens = list(tokenize.generate_tokens(io.StringIO(source).readline))
for tok in tokens:
    print(tok)

# 2. AST
tree = ast.parse(source)
print(ast.dump(tree, indent=2))

# 3. Bytecode
code = compile(source, "<string>", "exec")
dis.dis(code)
•

4.2 dis Module — Disassembling Functions

import dis

def example(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i * i
    return total

dis.dis(example)
# Output shows bytecode instructions:
# LOAD_CONST, STORE_FAST, LOAD_GLOBAL, LOAD_FAST, CALL_FUNCTION,
# GET_ITER, FOR_ITER, BINARY_MULTIPLY, INPLACE_ADD, etc.

# Compare two implementations to see why one is faster
def concat_loop(items):
    result = ""
    for item in items:
        result += str(item)
    return result

def concat_join(items):
    return "".join(str(item) for item in items)

dis.dis(concat_loop)   # more bytecodes, O(n²) string copies
dis.dis(concat_join)   # fewer bytecodes, O(n) via join
•

4.3 Peephole Optimizer & Constant Folding

import dis

# Constant folding — computed at compile time
def foo():
    x = 2 * 3 * 7       # folded to 42 at compile time
    y = "hello" * 3      # folded to "hellohellohello"
    z = (1, 2, 3)        # stored as constant tuple
    return x + len(z)

dis.dis(foo)
# LOAD_CONST 42  (not 2, 3, 7 separately)

# What IS NOT folded:
# - List/dict literals (mutable — must create new each time)
# - String concatenation beyond certain lengths
# - Anything involving function calls
•

4.4 __code__ Object Attributes

def example(a, b, c=10):
    x = a + b
    y = x * c
    return y

code = example.__code__
print(code.co_varnames)    # ('a', 'b', 'c', 'x', 'y')
print(code.co_consts)      # (None, 10)
print(code.co_argcount)    # 3
print(code.co_nlocals)     # 5
print(code.co_stacksize)   # max stack depth needed
print(code.co_filename)    # source file
print(code.co_firstlineno) # first line number
print(code.co_flags)       # bitmap flags (optimized, generator, etc.)
print(code.co_freevars)    # closure variables
print(code.co_cellvars)    # variables used in nested functions
•

4.5 sys.settrace / sys.setprofile

import sys

def trace_calls(frame, event, arg):
    """Simple call tracer."""
    if event == "call":
        print(f"Call: {frame.f_code.co_name} in {frame.f_code.co_filename}:{frame.f_lineno}")
    elif event == "return":
        print(f"Return: {frame.f_code.co_name} → {arg}")
    return trace_calls  # return itself to trace lines within

sys.settrace(trace_calls)
# ... run code ...
sys.settrace(None)  # disable

# sys.setprofile — lighter, only call/return/exception events
def profiler(frame, event, arg):
    if event == "call":
        print(f"→ {frame.f_code.co_name}")
    elif event == "return":
        print(f"← {frame.f_code.co_name}")

sys.setprofile(profiler)
•

4.6 Python Memory Layout

Every Python object (PyObject):
┌──────────────┐
│ ob_refcnt    │  ← reference count (Py_ssize_t)
│ ob_type      │  ← pointer to type object
│ ...data...   │  ← object-specific data
└──────────────┘

# Check with sys
import sys
x = 42
print(sys.getrefcount(x))   # reference count (+1 for the call itself)
print(sys.getsizeof(x))     # bytes: 28 for int

print(sys.getsizeof([]))         # 56 bytes (empty list)
print(sys.getsizeof([1,2,3]))    # 80 bytes
print(sys.getsizeof({}))         # 64 bytes (empty dict)
print(sys.getsizeof("hello"))    # 54 bytes

# id() returns memory address in CPython
print(id(x))  # memory address
print(hex(id(x)))

# Small integer caching: -5 to 256 are pre-allocated
a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)  # True (same object)
a = 257
b = 257
print(a is b)  # False (different objects) — usually
•

4.7 Why Certain Patterns Are Faster

import dis

# 1. Local variables are faster than globals (LOAD_FAST vs LOAD_GLOBAL)
x = 10
def slow():
    return x + x  # LOAD_GLOBAL x

def fast():
    y = x          # LOAD_GLOBAL once
    return y + y   # LOAD_FAST y, LOAD_FAST y

# 2. dict.get() vs try/except — for missing keys
d = {"a": 1}
# Faster for common misses:
v = d.get("b", 0)
# Slower for common misses:
try:
    v = d["b"]
except KeyError:
    v = 0

# 3. Membership testing: set vs list
# set:  O(1) — CONTAINS_OP uses hash table
# list: O(n) — CONTAINS_OP iterates
items_set = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
items_list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
x in items_set   # fast
x in items_list   # slow for large lists

def fib(n: int) -> int:

    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

6.4 Optimizing a Data Pipeline

# Before: Pure Python — slow
def process_records(records: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    for record in records:
        if record["value"] > 0:
            results.append({
                "id": record["id"],
                "score": record["value"] ** 0.5,
                "label": record["category"].lower(),
            })
    return results

# After: NumPy vectorized — fast
import numpy as np

def process_records_vectorized(ids, values, categories):
    mask = values > 0
    return {
        "ids": ids[mask],
        "scores": np.sqrt(values[mask]),
        "labels": np.char.lower(categories[mask]),
    }

# After: Numba JIT — fastest for numeric
from numba import njit

@njit
def compute_scores(values):
    n = len(values)
    scores = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        if values[i] > 0:
            scores[i] = values[i] ** 0.5
        else:
            scores[i] = 0.0
    return scores

7.1 httpx — Modern Async HTTP Client

import httpx

# Synchronous
response = httpx.get("https://api.example.com/predict")
print(response.json())

# Async
async def call_model_api():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        base_url="https://ml-api.example.com",
        timeout=httpx.Timeout(30.0, connect=5.0),
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer token"},
    ) as client:
        # Single request
        resp = await client.post("/predict", json={"text": "hello"})
        result = resp.json()

        # Concurrent requests
        import asyncio
        tasks = [
            client.post("/predict", json={"text": t})
            for t in ["hello", "world", "test"]
        ]
        responses = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
        return [r.json() for r in responses]

# Streaming (for LLM token streaming)
async def stream_tokens():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        async with client.stream("POST", "/generate", json={"prompt": "Hello"}) as resp:
            async for chunk in resp.aiter_text():
                print(chunk, end="", flush=True)

# Retry with tenacity
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential

@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_exponential(min=1, max=10))
async def reliable_predict(client, text):
    resp = await client.post("/predict", json={"text": text})
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()

7.2 WebSocket Programming

# Server (using FastAPI)
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect

app = FastAPI()

class ConnectionManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.active: list[WebSocket] = []

    async def connect(self, ws: WebSocket):
        await ws.accept()
        self.active.append(ws)

    def disconnect(self, ws: WebSocket):
        self.active.remove(ws)

    async def broadcast(self, message: str):
        for conn in self.active:
            await conn.send_text(message)

manager = ConnectionManager()

@app.websocket("/ws/predictions")
async def prediction_stream(ws: WebSocket):
    await manager.connect(ws)
    try:
        while True:
            data = await ws.receive_json()
            result = run_model(data["text"])
            await ws.send_json({"prediction": result})
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        manager.disconnect(ws)

# Client
import websockets
import asyncio
import json

async def ws_client():
    async with websockets.connect("ws://localhost:8000/ws/predictions") as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"text": "Hello ML"}))
        response = json.loads(await ws.recv())
        print(response)

7.3 asyncio Protocols and Transports

import asyncio

class EchoProtocol(asyncio.Protocol):
    def connection_made(self, transport):
        self.transport = transport
        peername = transport.get_extra_info("peername")
        print(f"Connection from {peername}")

    def data_received(self, data):
        message = data.decode()
        print(f"Received: {message}")
        self.transport.write(data)  # echo back

    def connection_lost(self, exc):
        print("Connection closed")

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    server = await loop.create_server(EchoProtocol, "0.0.0.0", 8888)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

7.4 gRPC with Python (Model Serving)

// prediction.proto
syntax = "proto3";

service PredictionService {
    rpc Predict (PredictRequest) returns (PredictResponse);
    rpc StreamPredict (PredictRequest) returns (stream PredictResponse);
}

message PredictRequest {
    string text = 1;
    string model_name = 2;
}

message PredictResponse {
    string label = 1;
    float score = 2;
}
# Server
import grpc
from concurrent import futures
import prediction_pb2
import prediction_pb2_grpc

class PredictionServicer(prediction_pb2_grpc.PredictionServiceServicer):
    def Predict(self, request, context):
        # Run ML inference
        label, score = model.predict(request.text)
        return prediction_pb2.PredictResponse(label=label, score=score)

    def StreamPredict(self, request, context):
        # Streaming response (e.g., token-by-token)
        for token in model.generate(request.text):
            yield prediction_pb2.PredictResponse(label=token, score=1.0)

def serve():
    server = grpc.server(futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10))
    prediction_pb2_grpc.add_PredictionServiceServicer_to_server(
        PredictionServicer(), server
    )
    server.add_insecure_port("[::]:50051")
    server.start()
    server.wait_for_termination()

# Client
async def grpc_client():
    async with grpc.aio.insecure_channel("localhost:50051") as channel:
        stub = prediction_pb2_grpc.PredictionServiceStub(channel)
        response = await stub.Predict(
            prediction_pb2.PredictRequest(text="hello", model_name="bert")
        )
        print(f"Label: {response.label}, Score: {response.score}")

        # Streaming
        async for resp in stub.StreamPredict(
            prediction_pb2.PredictRequest(text="generate this")
        ):
            print(resp.label, end="", flush=True)
Interview Questions — Debugging & Security
•

Q1: How would you debug a model that produces NaN loss during training?

Add NaN checksCheck inputsGradient normsLearning rateMixed precisionNumerical stability

A: Systematic approach: 1. Add NaN checks: torch.isnan(loss) after forward pass — breakpoint() when triggered 2. Check inputs: print(batch.min(), batch.max()) — look for extreme values or NaN in data 3. Gradient norms: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_() — exploding gradients cause NaN 4. Learning rate: Too high LR → divergence. Reduce by 10x and retry 5. Mixed precision: FP16 overflow — use torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler with proper settings 6. Numerical stability: Use log_softmax instead of log(softmax), add epsilon to divisions 7. Bisect: Disable components (dropout, normalization) to isolate the source

•

Q2: Why is pickle.loads() on untrusted data dangerous, and what are alternatives?

JSON/msgspecsafetensorsprotobuf/msgpackyaml.safeload()

A: pickle executes arbitrary Python during deserialization via the __reduce__ protocol. An attacker can craft a payload that runs os.system("rm -rf /") or opens a reverse shell when unpickled. Alternatives: - JSON/msgspec: Safe, fast, widely supported - safetensors: For ML model weights — no code execution - protobuf/msgpack: Binary formats without code execution - yaml.safe_load(): Instead of yaml.load() - Never unpickle data from untrusted sources (user uploads, network, shared storage without verification).

•

Q3: Explain the CPython compilation pipeline.

TokenizerParserCompiler

A: Source → Tokens (tokenizer) → AST (PEG parser) → Bytecode (compiler) → Execution (VM/ceval.c). - Tokenizer: Splits source into tokens (keywords, names, operators) - Parser: Builds Abstract Syntax Tree using PEG grammar (Python 3.9+) - Compiler: Traverses AST, emits bytecode instructions, applies peephole optimizations (constant folding, dead code elimination) - VM: Stack-based interpreter executes bytecodes in ceval.c. Each frame has a value stack, local variables array, and code object. - Inspect with: tokenize, ast.parse(), compile(), dis.dis()

•

Q4: Compare uv, Poetry, and pip for dependency management.

pipPoetry

A: - pip: Stdlib-adjacent, no lockfile, slow resolver, no env management. Fine for simple scripts. - Poetry: Mature lockfile (poetry.lock), good resolver, manages venvs. Slower install. Widely adopted. - uv: Written in Rust, 10–100x faster than pip. Has lockfile (uv.lock), manages Python versions, compatible with pip CLI. Rapidly becoming the standard. - For new projects, uv is recommended for speed and features. Poetry remains solid for teams already using it. pip alone is only for the simplest use cases.

•

Q5: How would you implement secure secret management in an ML application?

Never hardcodeEnvironment variablespydantic-settingsSecrets managerRotate secretsgitignore

A: 1. Never hardcode secrets in source code or config files committed to git 2. Environment variables for simple deployments: os.environ["API_KEY"] 3. pydantic-settings for structured loading from env + .env files with type validation 4. Secrets manager in production: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager 5. Rotate secrets regularly; use short-lived tokens where possible 6. .gitignore must include .env, *.pem, any secret files 7. Audit: Use pip-audit and detect-secrets (pre-commit hook) to catch accidental leaks 8. Principle of least privilege: Each service gets only the secrets it needs

Interview Questions — Logging, Internals & Networking
•

Q6: What are the advantages of structured logging over print/basic logging?

Machine-parseableContext propagationCorrelation IDsFiltering and alertingNo regex neededstructlog

A: - Machine-parseable: JSON output can be queried in ELK, CloudWatch Insights, Datadog - Context propagation: Bound loggers carry request_id, user_id automatically across function calls - Correlation IDs: Trace requests across microservices - Filtering and alerting: Query level=error AND latency_ms > 1000 in production - No regex needed: Structured fields vs. parsing free-text log lines - structlog is the standard Python library: processors pipeline, contextvars integration, stdlib compatibility

•

Q7: When would you use gRPC over REST for model serving?

gRPC advantagesREST advantagesUse gRPC whenUse REST when

A: - gRPC advantages: Binary protocol (protobuf) = smaller payloads and faster serialization, bidirectional streaming (token-by-token generation), strong typing via .proto schemas, HTTP/2 multiplexing, code generation for client/server - REST advantages: Browser-friendly, simpler debugging (curl/Postman), wider ecosystem, easier caching - Use gRPC when: Internal microservice communication, high-throughput inference, streaming responses (LLM generation), polyglot environments needing generated clients - Use REST when: Public APIs, browser clients, simple request-response, team familiarity

Testing and Debugging62 sections

Testing & Debugging — Complete Python Reference

Scope: unittest and pytest (fixtures, parametrize, markers, mocking, coverage), doctest, property-based testing, test doubles (stub/spy/fake/mock), the test pyramid, pdb/breakpoint()/debugpy interactive debugging, post-mortem and remote debugging, logging for debugging, profiling (cProfile, tracemalloc), tracing, plus secure-coding essentials (OWASP, pickle safety, injection, secrets, crypto, dependency scanning).

1. Why Test? The Test Pyramid

Automated tests catch regressions, document intended behaviour, and give the confidence to refactor. The test pyramid describes the healthy ratio of test types:

            ╱╲        End-to-End (few, slow, brittle)
           ╱  ╲       — full system through the UI/API
          ╱────╲
         ╱      ╲     Integration (some, medium speed)
        ╱        ╲    — multiple components together (DB, files, services)
       ╱──────────╲
      ╱            ╲  Unit (many, fast, isolated)
     ╱______________╲ — one function/class, no I/O, mock dependencies
TypeSpeedScopeWhen it fails, the bug is…
Unitmssingle function/class…in that function
Integrationsecondsseveral units + I/O…in how units interact / config
End-to-Endminuteswhole application…somewhere (hardest to localize)

Guiding principles: tests should be fast, isolated (no shared state), deterministic (no flakiness), and readable (a failing test name should tell you what broke). Follow Arrange-Act-Assert structure inside each test.

2. unittest — The Standard Library Framework

unittest ships with Python (xUnit-style). Tests are methods named test_* inside a TestCase subclass, using self.assert* methods.

import unittest

def calculator(a, b, op):
    if op == '+': return a + b
    if op == '-': return a - b
    if op == '*': return a * b
    if op == '/':
        if b == 0:
            raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero")
        return a / b
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown operator: {op}")

class TestCalculator(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add(self):
        self.assertEqual(calculator(2, 3, '+'), 5)

    def test_divide(self):
        self.assertAlmostEqual(calculator(10, 3, '/'), 3.333, places=2)

    def test_divide_by_zero(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            calculator(5, 0, '/')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
# Ran 3 tests in 0.001s — OK
•

Common Assertion Methods

MethodChecks
assertEqual(a, b)a == b
assertNotEqual(a, b)a != b
assertTrue(x) / assertFalse(x)truthiness
assertIs(a, b) / assertIsNotidentity (a is b)
assertIsNone(x) / assertIsNotNonex is None
assertIn(a, b) / assertNotInmembership
assertIsInstance(a, cls)isinstance(a, cls)
assertAlmostEqual(a, b, places=7)floats equal to N decimal places
assertRaises(Err)context manager — body raises Err
assertRaisesRegex(Err, regex)raises Err whose message matches
•

setUp / tearDown (Fixtures)

setUp runs before every test method; tearDown after. Use them to build/destroy per-test state. Class-level equivalents are setUpClass/tearDownClass (run once per class).

import unittest

class Stack:
    def __init__(self): self._items = []
    def push(self, x): self._items.append(x)
    def pop(self): return self._items.pop()
    def size(self): return len(self._items)

class TestStack(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):                 # fresh stack for each test
        self.stack = Stack()
        self.stack.push(1)
        self.stack.push(2)

    def tearDown(self):
        self.stack = None

    def test_pop(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.stack.pop(), 2)
        self.assertEqual(self.stack.size(), 1)

    def test_push(self):
        self.stack.push(3)
        self.assertEqual(self.stack.size(), 3)
•

subTest — Loop-Based Parametrization

self.subTest() reports each iteration independently, so one failing case does not hide the others.

class TestPalindrome(unittest.TestCase):
    cases = [("racecar", True), ("hello", False), ("", True), ("ab", False)]

    def test_palindromes(self):
        for text, expected in self.cases:
            with self.subTest(text=text):
                cleaned = text.lower().replace(" ", "")
                self.assertEqual(cleaned == cleaned[::-1], expected)
3. pytest — The Modern Standard

pytest is the most popular framework: it auto-discovers test_* functions in test_*.py files, uses plain assert (rich failure introspection — no assertEqual boilerplate), and has a powerful fixture/plugin ecosystem.

# test_stack.py
import pytest

class Stack:
    def __init__(self): self._items = []
    def push(self, x): self._items.append(x)
    def pop(self):
        if not self._items:
            raise IndexError("Pop from empty stack")
        return self._items.pop()
    def is_empty(self): return len(self._items) == 0

def test_push_and_pop():
    s = Stack()
    s.push(1); s.push(2)
    assert s.pop() == 2
    assert s.pop() == 1

def test_pop_empty_raises():
    s = Stack()
    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        s.pop()
pytest                      # discover & run everything
pytest test_stack.py -v     # verbose, one line per test
pytest -k "pop"             # only tests whose name matches "pop"
pytest -x                   # stop after first failure
pytest --tb=short           # shorter tracebacks
pytest -q                   # quiet
pytest --lf                 # rerun only last-failed tests
•

Float Comparison: pytest.approx

def test_float():
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)            # True (handles FP error)
    assert 3.333 == pytest.approx(10 / 3, rel=1e-2)   # relative tolerance
•

Markers

Markers tag tests for selection or special handling.

import pytest, sys

@pytest.mark.slow                                  # custom marker (register in pyproject)
def test_big_computation(): ...

@pytest.mark.skip(reason="not implemented yet")
def test_future(): ...

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason="POSIX only")
def test_posix(): ...

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="known bug, fix pending")  # expected to fail
def test_known_bug():
    assert buggy() == 42

# Run only fast tests:  pytest -m "not slow"
# pyproject.toml — register markers to avoid warnings
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-v --tb=short"
markers = ["slow: marks tests as slow"]
4. Fixtures

pytest fixtures provide setup/teardown via dependency injection: declare a fixture once, then any test that names it as a parameter receives the value. Code before yield is setup; code after is teardown.

import pytest
import sqlite3

@pytest.fixture
def db_connection():
    """In-memory DB seeded with test data; closed after the test."""
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, age INTEGER)")
    conn.executemany("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES (?, ?)",
                     [("Alice", 30), ("Bob", 25)])
    conn.commit()
    yield conn          # ← test runs here
    conn.close()        # ← teardown

@pytest.fixture
def user_repo(db_connection):          # fixtures can depend on fixtures
    class UserRepo:
        def __init__(self, conn): self.conn = conn
        def get_all(self): return self.conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users").fetchall()
    return UserRepo(db_connection)

def test_get_all(user_repo):           # just name the fixture to use it
    assert len(user_repo.get_all()) == 2
•

Fixture Scope

Control how often a fixture is created with scope:

ScopeCreated once per…
"function"each test (default)
"class"test class
"module".py file
"package"package
"session"whole test run
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def http_client():
    client = make_expensive_client()
    yield client
    client.close()
•

Built-in Fixtures

def test_save_load(tmp_path):          # tmp_path: a unique Path per test
    f = tmp_path / "model.pkl"
    f.write_bytes(b"data")
    assert f.read_bytes() == b"data"

def test_env(monkeypatch):             # monkeypatch: safely patch env/attrs
    monkeypatch.setenv("API_KEY", "test")
    monkeypatch.setattr("mymod.timeout", 0)

def test_output(capsys):               # capsys: capture stdout/stderr
    print("hello")
    assert capsys.readouterr().out == "hello\n"

conftest.py: fixtures placed here are shared across the whole test directory without importing — pytest discovers them automatically.

5. Parametrized Tests

Run the same test body against many inputs; each row is reported as a separate test.

import pytest

def is_palindrome(s):
    cleaned = ''.join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum())
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("input_str, expected", [
    ("racecar", True),
    ("hello", False),
    ("A man a plan a canal Panama", True),
    ("", True),
    ("Was it a car or a cat I saw?", True),
])
def test_palindrome(input_str, expected):
    assert is_palindrome(input_str) == expected
# 5 test cases, each shown separately in -v output

Stack parametrize decorators for a Cartesian product:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("x", [1, 2])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("y", [10, 20])
def test_combos(x, y):       # runs 4 times: (1,10) (1,20) (2,10) (2,20)
    assert x + y > 0

The unittest equivalent is subTest (see §2).

6. Testing Exceptions
# ── pytest ────────────────────────────────────────────────
import pytest

def divide(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        raise ZeroDivisionError("Cannot divide by zero")
    return a / b

def test_divide_by_zero():
    with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError):
        divide(10, 0)

def test_message():
    with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError, match="Cannot divide"):  # regex on message
        divide(1, 0)

def test_inspect_exception():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError) as exc_info:
        int("not a number")
    assert "invalid literal" in str(exc_info.value)

# ── unittest ──────────────────────────────────────────────
import unittest

class TestBank(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_overdraft(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError) as ctx:
            withdraw(100, 200)
        self.assertIn("insufficient", str(ctx.exception).lower())
7. Mocking & Test Doubles

A test double replaces a real dependency (network, DB, clock) so the unit under test runs in isolation. The taxonomy:

DoublePurpose
Dummypassed but never used (fills a parameter)
Stubreturns canned answers to calls made during the test
Spya stub that also records how it was called
Mockpre-programmed with expectations; verifies interactions
Fakea working but lightweight implementation (e.g. in-memory DB/cache)
•

unittest.mock

from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

class WeatherApp:
    def __init__(self, service): self.service = service
    def get_forecast(self, city):
        temp = self.service.get_temperature(city)
        return "Hot" if temp > 30 else "Cold"

# Mock: program return value, then verify the interaction
def test_hot_weather():
    mock_service = Mock()
    mock_service.get_temperature.return_value = 35
    app = WeatherApp(mock_service)

    assert app.get_forecast("NYC") == "Hot"
    mock_service.get_temperature.assert_called_once_with("NYC")  # interaction check
•

patch — Replace a Name in Its Namespace

patch temporarily swaps an attribute for a Mock, restoring it afterwards. Patch where the name is looked up, not where it is defined.

import requests

def fetch_user(user_id):
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}").json()

# As a context manager
def test_fetch_user():
    with patch("mymodule.requests.get") as mock_get:
        mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {"id": 1, "name": "Alice"}
        assert fetch_user(1)["name"] == "Alice"

# As a decorator (mock is injected as an argument)
@patch("mymodule.requests.get")
def test_fetch_user_decorated(mock_get):
    mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {"id": 2}
    assert fetch_user(2)["id"] == 2

# Patch an object's method directly
def test_method():
    service = WeatherApp(Mock())
    with patch.object(service, "get_forecast", return_value="Warm"):
        assert service.get_forecast("X") == "Warm"
•

side_effect, MagicMock, and Assertions

from unittest.mock import Mock, MagicMock, call

m = Mock()
m.side_effect = [1, 2, 3]          # successive return values
assert (m(), m(), m()) == (1, 2, 3)

m2 = Mock(side_effect=ValueError)  # raise on call
# m2()  → raises ValueError

mm = MagicMock()                   # supports dunders: len(), [], context mgr, etc.
mm.__len__.return_value = 5
assert len(mm) == 5

spy = Mock()
spy.info("a"); spy.info("b")
assert spy.info.call_count == 2
spy.info.assert_has_calls([call("a"), call("b")])
spy.error.assert_not_called()
•

Fakes vs Stubs (Hand-Rolled)

# Stub — canned response only
stub_db = Mock()
stub_db.find_user.return_value = {"name": "Alice", "role": "admin"}

# Fake — real working logic, just lightweight
class FakeCache:
    def __init__(self): self.store = {}
    def get(self, key): return self.store.get(key)
    def set(self, key, value): self.store[key] = value

cache = FakeCache()
cache.set("x", 42)
assert cache.get("x") == 42 and cache.get("y") is None

pytest-mock plugin gives a mocker fixture that wraps unittest.mock with automatic teardown: mocker.patch("mod.func", return_value=1).

8. Test Coverage

Coverage measures which lines/branches the tests execute. It reveals untested code — but 100% coverage does not prove correctness (you can execute a line without asserting its effect).

pip install pytest-cov            # or: pip install coverage

pytest --cov=myapp                              # coverage for the myapp package
pytest --cov=myapp --cov-report=term-missing    # show line numbers not covered
pytest --cov=myapp --cov-report=html            # browsable htmlcov/ report
pytest --cov=myapp --cov-fail-under=80          # fail CI if below 80%
# Module under test, plus tests aiming for full branch coverage
def fibonacci(n):
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Negative input")   # branch A
    if n <= 1:
        return n                              # branch B
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b                                  # branch C

import unittest
class TestFib(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_base(self):     self.assertEqual(fibonacci(1), 1)    # B
    def test_normal(self):   self.assertEqual(fibonacci(10), 55)  # C
    def test_negative(self):                                       # A
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            fibonacci(-1)
# pytest --cov=mymod --cov-report=term-missing  → 100%, no missing lines

Prefer branch coverage (--cov-branch) over line coverage: it checks that both sides of each if are taken.

9. doctest

doctest runs the interactive examples written in docstrings, keeping documentation and behaviour in sync.

def reverse_words(sentence):
    """Reverse the order of words in a sentence.

    >>> reverse_words("hello world")
    'world hello'
    >>> reverse_words("")
    ''
    >>> reverse_words("single")
    'single'
    """
    return ' '.join(sentence.split()[::-1])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import doctest
    doctest.testmod(verbose=True)
# Run: python module.py        (or)   python -m doctest module.py -v

Useful directives: # doctest: +SKIP, +ELLIPSIS (use ... to match variable output), +NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE. Best for small, pure functions; not a substitute for a real test suite.

10. Property-Based & Fuzz Testing

Instead of hand-picking examples, property-based testing asserts invariants over generated inputs. Hypothesis generates cases and shrinks any failure to a minimal counterexample.

# pip install hypothesis
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

def sort_list(lst):
    return sorted(lst)

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_preserves_length(lst):
    assert len(sort_list(lst)) == len(lst)

@given(st.lists(st.integers(), min_size=1))
def test_sort_is_ordered(lst):
    result = sort_list(lst)
    assert all(result[i] <= result[i+1] for i in range(len(result) - 1))

@given(st.text())
def test_reverse_involution(s):
    assert s[::-1][::-1] == s          # reversing twice = identity

Common invariants to test: round-trip (decode(encode(x)) == x), idempotence (f(f(x)) == f(x)), commutativity, and comparison with a slow reference implementation.

•

Lightweight Fuzzing (No Dependency)

import random, string, json

def fuzz(func, generator, iterations=500):
    failures = []
    for _ in range(iterations):
        x = generator()
        try:
            func(x)
        except Exception as e:
            failures.append((x, str(e)))
    return failures

rand_str = lambda: ''.join(random.choices(string.printable, k=random.randint(0, 50)))
fails = fuzz(json.loads, rand_str)   # expect many — random text isn't valid JSON
print(f"{500 - len(fails)}/500 handled without crashing the harness")
11. Other Testing Patterns
•

Integration Test with Temp Files

import unittest, tempfile, os, json

class ConfigManager:
    def __init__(self, path): self.path = path
    def save(self, cfg):
        with open(self.path, "w") as f: json.dump(cfg, f)
    def load(self):
        with open(self.path) as f: return json.load(f)

class TestConfig(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.tmp = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".json", delete=False)
        self.tmp.close()
        self.mgr = ConfigManager(self.tmp.name)

    def tearDown(self):
        os.unlink(self.tmp.name)

    def test_round_trip(self):
        cfg = {"key": "value", "count": 42}
        self.mgr.save(cfg)
        self.assertEqual(self.mgr.load(), cfg)
•

Snapshot Testing

Capture a reference output once; later runs assert nothing changed (great for serialized structures, rendered templates).

import json, os

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, directory="__snapshots__"):
        os.makedirs(directory, exist_ok=True)
        self.dir = directory

    def assert_match(self, name, data, update=False):
        path = os.path.join(self.dir, f"{name}.json")
        serialized = json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True)
        if update or not os.path.exists(path):
            with open(path, "w") as f: f.write(serialized)
            return                                   # first run: record baseline
        with open(path) as f: expected = f.read()
        assert serialized == expected, f"Snapshot '{name}' changed"
•

Test Data Builder / Factory

Build valid test objects with sensible defaults, overriding only what matters per test.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str = "Anonymous"
    email: str = "anon@test.com"
    age: int = 0
    roles: list = field(default_factory=list)

class UserBuilder:
    def __init__(self): self._u = User()
    def with_name(self, n): self._u.name = n; return self
    def with_roles(self, *r): self._u.roles = list(r); return self
    def build(self): return self._u

admin = UserBuilder().with_name("Alice").with_roles("admin").build()
# Builders keep tests readable: only the relevant field is set.
•

Design by Contract (Pre/Post-conditions)

from functools import wraps

def contract(pre=None, post=None):
    def deco(func):
        @wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            if pre:  assert pre(*args, **kwargs), f"Precondition failed: {func.__name__}"
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            if post: assert post(result), f"Postcondition failed: {func.__name__}"
            return result
        return wrapper
    return deco

@contract(pre=lambda x, y: x >= 0 and y >= 0, post=lambda r: r >= 0)
def safe_divide(x, y):
    return x / y if y else 0

safe_divide(10, 3)     # 3.333...
# safe_divide(-1, 2)   → AssertionError: Precondition failed
12. Interactive Debugging — pdb & breakpoint()

pdb is the built-in interactive debugger. Since Python 3.7, breakpoint() is the preferred entry point — it honours the PYTHONBREAKPOINT environment variable.

import pdb; pdb.set_trace()     # classic
import ipdb; ipdb.set_trace()   # ipdb: colour + tab-completion (pip install ipdb)
breakpoint()                    # 3.7+ preferred — configurable, no import needed
•

Command Reference

overintodown
CommandAction
n (next)Execute next line (step over calls)
s (step)Step into a function call
c (continue)Run until the next breakpoint
r (return)Run until the current function returns
l / llList source around line / full current function
p expr / ppPrint / pretty-print an expression
w (where)Print the stack trace
u / dMove up / down one stack frame
b N / b funcSet a breakpoint at line N / function entry
b file:NBreakpoint in another file
tbreak NTemporary breakpoint (auto-cleared after first hit)
condition N exprBreak at breakpoint N only when expr is truthy
commands NRun a list of commands automatically when breakpoint N hits
cl / cl NClear all / clear breakpoint N
a (args)Print arguments of the current function
interactDrop into a full interactive shell in the current frame
!stmtExecute a statement (use when a var shadows a command)
q (quit)Abort the program
•

Conditional Breakpoints

def train_step(batch_idx, loss):
    if batch_idx == 500 and loss > 10.0:

    ...
# Or inside pdb:   b 42, loss > 10.0    (break at line 42 only when loss > 10)

def hook(exc_type, exc_value, exc_tb):

14. Logging for Debugging

print is fine for throwaway debugging, but logging gives levels, timestamps, module names, and the ability to route output to files — without editing call sites.

import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.DEBUG,
    format="%(asctime)s | %(name)s | %(levelname)-8s | %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
    handlers=[logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)],
)
logger = logging.getLogger("app")

def process_data(data):
    logger.info("Processing %d items", len(data))
    results = []
    for i, item in enumerate(data):
        logger.debug("item %d: %r", i, item)
        try:
            results.append(item["value"] * 2)
        except (KeyError, TypeError) as e:
            logger.warning("Skipping item %d: %s", i, e)
    logger.info("Done: %d/%d succeeded", len(results), len(data))
    return results

process_data([{"value": 10}, {"bad": "data"}, {"value": 30}])
# 14:02:01 | app | INFO     | Processing 3 items
# 14:02:01 | app | WARNING  | Skipping item 1: 'value'
# 14:02:01 | app | INFO     | Done: 2/3 succeeded
•

Levels & Debugging Tips

lazy %-formattingstructlog

DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL. Set the threshold once; ship at INFO, drop to DEBUG to investigate.

logger.exception("Operation failed")   # ERROR + full traceback (call inside except)
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)   # flip a single line to reveal debug logs

Use lazy %-formatting (logger.debug("x=%s", x)) so the string is only built if the level is enabled. For machine-parseable JSON logs, correlation IDs, and bound context across async requests, use structlog (see the Logging reference).

15. Profiling & Performance Debugging

"Premature optimization is the root of all evil." Profile first, then optimize the proven hotspot.

•

Timing — timeit

import timeit
timeit.timeit("sum(range(1000))", number=10000)   # micro-benchmark, seconds
•

Function-Level CPU — cProfile

import cProfile, pstats, io
from functools import wraps

def profile(func):
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        pr = cProfile.Profile()
        pr.enable()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        pr.disable()
        s = io.StringIO()
        pstats.Stats(pr, stream=s).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(10)
        print(s.getvalue())
        return result
    return wrapper

@profile
def matrix_multiply(n):
    A = [[i + j for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * A[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]

matrix_multiply(50)   # prints ncalls / tottime / cumtime per function

# CLI alternative (no code change):
#   python -m cProfile -s cumulative script.py
•

Line-by-Line & Sampling Profilers

Memory — tracemalloc

import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
data = [{"id": i, "values": list(range(100))} for i in range(1000)]
snapshot = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in snapshot.statistics("lineno")[:5]:
    print(stat)                                  # top allocation sites
current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(f"Current: {current/1024:.0f} KB, Peak: {peak/1024:.0f} KB")
tracemalloc.stop()
•

Performance Wins (in order of impact)

  1. Choose the right data structure — set/dict membership is O(1) vs O(n) for lists.
  2. ''.join(parts) instead of += in a loop (avoids O(n²) string copies).
  3. List/generator comprehensions over manual append loops.
  4. functools.lru_cache for expensive, repeated, pure calls.
  5. Vectorize numeric work with NumPy; avoid per-element Python loops.
  6. Generators for large datasets (lazy, constant memory).

import sys

def trace_calls(frame, event, arg):
    if event == "call":
        print(f"Call: {frame.f_code.co_name}:{frame.f_lineno}")
    elif event == "return":
        print(f"Return: {frame.f_code.co_name} → {arg!r}")
    return trace_calls

sys.settrace(trace_calls)
# ... run code ...
sys.settrace(None)        # disable

Disassembly — Why One Version Is Faster

import dis
def concat_loop(items):
    s = ""
    for x in items: s += str(x)        # O(n²) string copies
    return s
def concat_join(items):
    return "".join(str(x) for x in items)  # O(n)
dis.dis(concat_loop)   # many INPLACE_ADD ops
dis.dis(concat_join)   # tighter bytecode
